Chapter II 
VIGILANCE ADMINISTRATION IN CENTRAL PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES 
(CPSEs) AND PUBLIC SECTOR BANKS (PSBs) 
 
2. CPSEs account for public invest ment of more than Rs. 1 2 lakh c rores, spread over 
320 Enterprises. The original purposes, for which these Enterprises were set up, varied and 
included such objectives as: 
(a) Setting up of  infrastructure for rapid industrial growth; 
(b) Creation of additional employment opportunities; 
(c) Facilitation of balanced regional development; 
(d) Generation of surplus funds for further investment for  economic development; 
and 
(e) Reduction of disparities in income and wealth through  prevention of 
concentration of economic power in private hands. 
2.1 Over the years, the focus has shifted towards providing greater autonomy and 
ensuring greater transparency within the functioning of these enterprises.  Current thinking 
stresses the impor tance of these units becoming self -reliant and profitable ventures and 
building themselves around their strengths to face competitive challenges from the private 
sector. In the ultimate analysis, the vigilance function should not be organised so as to detr act 
from, impair, or inhibit commercial decision making within these Enterprises. 
2.2 However, t oday the PSEs in the country play a significant  
role in the economic and social development of the country. Further, their functions ranges 
from monopolistic nature like Railways, Atomic Energy, Life Insurance etc. to highly 
competitive fields like Banking , Insurance, Heavy Engineering,  etc. These undertakings are 
not just  regarded as large commercial undertakings judged on their comme rcial results but 
have wider objectives than commercial concerns of the private sector. They deal with  
tax payers’ money and are therefore accountable to the Parliament. They are subject to public 
criticism and criticism in the press. Unli ke the private co mmercial organization where 
individuals count more, in these public undertakings, the systems have to work more than 
individuals. Under such  circumstances, there is a need for a strong vigilance organization in 
the PSEs with a set of rules to regulate the conduct of the employees of these undertakings. 
Committee’s Study-visits for appraisal of Vigilance Administration in PSUs and PSBs: 
2.3 In the course of examination of the Subject , the Committee undertook a study -visit to 
Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata from 26 thto 31 st August, 2018 and to Hyderabad, Bengaluru 
and Mumbai from 14 th to 18 th January, 2020 and made an appraisal of the vigilance 
administration of several PSUs and PSBs. Detailed study tour reports of both the study visits 
of the Committee are placed at Annexure I and Annexure II.  
2.4 In the presence of officers from the concerned Ministries/Departments and DoPT, t he 
Committee had interaction with the representatives of the PS Us and PSBs on the subject. 
Detailed presentation s were made by them inter-alia highlighting their internal vigilance 

6 
 
mechanism, steps taken by them in strengthening vigilance administration, spreading 
awareness about vigilance amongst their stakeholders etc.  
2.5 The Committee was informed about the initiatives taken by the PSBs & PSUs  for 
strengthening preventive vigila nce viz., holding meetings on aspects of preventive vigilance 
with Branch Managers and Zonal Officials; conduction of  inspection in all branches; 
investigation of complaints & initiation of appropriate remedial Action; enhancing vigilance 
awareness and co mpliance level among the employees through CVO’s Monthly magazines 
and sharing of information through whatsapp Group to reach out  to all Managers and other 
officials of the PSBs/PSUs. 
2.6 The Committee was further informed as to how t echnology is being lev eraged to 
being about  transparency & reduc e corruption in the PSBs  viz. whistle blower portal 
(Intranet); off Site Monitoring System; implementation of controls in Core Banking Solution 
(CBS) for various Delegation of powers of the Branch officials, modifi cation in repayment 
schedule; issuance of Solvency Certificate through Finacle System etc.; concessions module 
for Trade Finance through Finacle System.  
2.7 The Committee was also informed that some PSBs /PSBs have implemented Integrity 
Pact and appointed Independent External Monitors (IEMs) to strengthen preventive vigilance. 
Quarterly Structured Meetings of IEMs with CVO & concerned Executives are conducted 
and Action Taken Report on the Minutes of the meetings is reviewed. Bank s and PSUs are 
also affecting rotational transfers as per the directions of CVC in respect of o fficers who are 
continuing beyond 3 years from the sensitive seat / post and not necessarily from the station. 
It was further informed that the Annual Confidential Reports of CV O is written by the MD & 
CEO and sent to the DFS, Ministry of Finance for review and for onward submission of the 
same to CVC as accepting authority. CVO and Vigilance Department officials also undergo 
periodical training for skill development. 
 
2.8 Some PSBs requested that the threshold limit for inv estigation of fraud cases by CBI  
may be increased from the present level of outstanding of Rs.3.00 Cr to a higher level which 
may be about Rs. 10 Cr or above. Further, it was also suggested that the realizable value of 
primary & collateral securities and probable cash recovery from other sources, if any, may be 
allowed to be deducted from the outstanding balance and on the remaining amount, up to 
about 50% provision may be made. This would enable Bankers to decl are such accounts as 
Fraud without delay.   
2.9 The Committee was also made to understand that there are instances where 
unscrupulous borrowers/middlemen raise high value credit by fudging financial statements, 
excess valuation of Primary & Collateral securities, obtaining clear legal opinion on defective 
documents in collusion with financial consultants/CA/Valuers/Advocates as the case may be. 
As Bankers generally depend on such professionals’ advice for decision making, it is 
suggested that in all such ca ses, if the loans and advances turn NPA solely due to above 
reasons/ irregularities, Bank officials may not be held accountable for the accounts turning 
into NPA. Further, legal framework s to be strengthened to take punitive action on such 
professionals by  implicating them in the CBI cases. Such measures may deter them from 
doing unscrupulous activities.  
2.10 The Committee was also informed that i n the recent past many frauds have come to 
the notice of Banks due to improper certification done by the TPEs a nd the Banks have failed 
to hold them accountable. To ensure accountability of TPEs, it was requested that a Code of 

7 
 
Conduct and a legally enforceable agreement should be executed by all these TPEs, so as to 
bring in better ethics and accountability on their part. 
2.11 Following points were also highlighted by PSUs/PSBs in their presentation: 
(i) The Committee was apprised by the top management of the PSUs/PSBs that their 
focus has shifted from punitive to preventive vigilance. They have leveraged 
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) for this purpose which inter-
alia includes online tende ring, bill tracking, e -procurement, e -auction, online 
filing and tracking of complains, etc. The Committee was also apprised that 
because of these steps, taken over the years, number of vigilance cases has gone 
down significantly. 
(ii) Further, as a part of pre ventive vigilance, ‘vigilance awareness weeks’ are 
organized regularly and the employees, clients, vendors, public etc. are made 
aware by holding seminars/lectures and publicizin g it through workshops, radio, 
whatsapp and SMS, etc. 
(iii) Notice Board has been displayed in all the Units, to sensitize the Public not to give 
bribe and to intimate demand of bribe to the Competent Authority. 
(iv) Vigilance activities and Vigilance related issues are being published through in -
house magazine. 
(v) Surprise inspections and audit of satellite offices are done on regular intervals to 
check any fraud at the cutting edge level.  
(vi) Various Complaints were referred to CVC, CBI, PMO, etc. Provision for internal 
and external audit including internal inspection of all Offices of PSUs and PSBs. 
(vii) Provision for property returns obtained from employees annually. 
(viii) Establishment of robust online grievance reporting and redressal mechanism 
adopted by all PSUs/PSBs including development of in -house data vigilance 
module. 
(ix) All procurements as per CVC gui delines. E-Tendering process as well as Reverse 
Auction system in place. 
Interaction with the representatives of the Government and CVC on the subject: 
2.12 The Committee held intensive deliberations with the  officials of  DoPT, CVC, DFS 
and Department of Public Enterprises on the subject. Views of the Government and CVC on 
various issues identified by the Committee, pertaining to the Subject , are summarised as 
under:  
(i) Recent initiatives undertaken by CVC to bring out transparen cy  
in Governance: 
(a) Leveraging Technology to Prevent Discretion and Corruption : C VC had 
adopted the strategy  ‘Leveraging Technology to Prevent Corruption’ since 
2004, wherein organisations are persuaded to adopt e -governance 
measures and computerise on priority all those activities which are 

8 
 
vulnerable to corruption.  Improv ing vigilance administration by 
leveraging technology, advocated by the Commission, h as been reported 
as a best practice by Organisation for Economic Co -operation and 
Development (OECD), Paris in 2009. Today, almost all procurements of 
Rs. 2 lakhs and above are made through e -procurement portal (now CP 
Portal and GeM) or by reverse auction  by the Central Government 
Departments / organisations which has brought in greater transparency and 
also reduced discretion as well as reduced cost of procurements. 
 
(b) Integrity in public procurement  - Integrity Pact : Since December, 2007, 
CVChas been  promoting the concept of Integrity Pact which involves 
signing of a pact between the procuring organisation and the bidders that 
they will not indulge in corrupt practices in the tendering, award and the 
execution of the contract. Public procurement being the g overnment 
activity most vulnerable to corruption has been a priority concern of the 
Commission.  Integrity Pact is intended to make public procurement 
transparent by binding both parties to ethical conduct. IP covers all 
activities related to the contract from pre-selection of bidders, bidding and 
contracting, implementation, completion and operation.  Independent 
External Monitors are nominated by the Commission to monitor the 
adherence to the pact by the two sides. Ministry of Finance, DoE, has also 
in Jul y, 2011, directed Ministries/Departments of the Govt. for 
implementation of Integrity Pact. More than 160 organisations including 
the Ministries conducting major procurements have adopted the Integrity 
Pact. Commission also recommends various reforms in pu blic 
procurement system from time to time to the government. 
(ii) On inordinate delay in completion of disciplinary proceeding: 
CVC has observed that a number of factors contribute to delay in completion of 
disciplinary proceedings, particularly in departmental inquiries. The Departmental 
inquiry is often delayed due to  lack of monitoring by D isciplinary Authority, non-
availability of documents, delay in inspection of documents, frequent adjournments, 
non-attendance of witnesses, court stay, change of IO/PO, etc. 
 
Normally, a vigilance case needs to be completed within a period of eighteen 
months (i.e. from the stage of complaint to  finalisation of disciplinary proceedings). 
The Commission has been issuing instructions for timely completion of disciplinary 
proceedings from time to time. It has also prescribed a schedule of time -limits vide 
its Circular dated 23.5.2000, subsequently r evised through ‘Model Time Limits’ 
published in para 7.47.2 of Vigilance Manual 2017,for various stages of activities 
right from receipt of complaint, its investigation, decisions by competent authorities 
as well as the conduct and finalisation of discipli nary proceedings against public 
servants.  All these activities are to be completed in eighteen months.  CVOs are 
required to submit monthly/quarterly reports in prescribed format. CVOs are 
required to submit monthly/quarterly reports in prescribed format. Besides this, the 
CVC regularly reviews the progress of disciplinary proceedings pending with the 
organisations / departments through Annual Review meetings which is also attended 
by the Secretaries /Chief Executives of the Departments/Organisations apart from 
the CVOs. 

9 
 
(iii) On previous Bank frauds: 
 
a) In matters of commission of frauds in a bank involving any culpability of 
staff/officers, the CVO is required to determine staff accountability, 
identify the pattern of fraud, and suggest preventive measures to curb  
recurrence of a particular modus operandi in individual cases of fraud. 
After fixing staff accountability, appropriate disciplinary action is 
recommended by the CVO under the relevant rules/regulations applicable 
to the staff/officers. In matters involvin g criminality either by staff or 
outsiders, reporting to concerned investigating agency is to be made by the 
designated administrative authorities in consultation with the CVO. The 
Commission has not come across any specific matter where the CVO has 
failed in his duties warranting any formal disciplinary proceedings. 
However, a few CVOs were found lacking in discharge of their functions 
have been reverted from the post of CVO. 
 
b) Frauds unearthed in Banks in the  recent past were the combined outcomes 
of syste m failure, mis -judgement as well as commercial lapses. For 
strengthening the vigilance system in banks to avert system failures, the  
Commission has been advocating  Standard Operating Procedures in 
various areas of management. To bring down the incidence of  mis-
judgement, the Commission has been advising improvement in the training 
provision for officials at various levels and also for job rotation from time 
to time so that officers are tuned to work in different areas of operations. 
To reduce the commercial  lapses affecting the banks and insurance 
companies, Commission has been advocating strict adherence to KYC 
norms, due diligence, proper monitoring, etc. 
 
(iv)    On Integrity Index: 
The Central Vigilance Commission has undertaken an initiative to develop an 
Integrity Index applicable to a wide range of Public Sector and Government 
Organizations. The development of Integrity Index is in line with the CVC’s 
broader strategy and emphasis on preventive measures. This is an exercise by the 
organizations for self -assessment of its policies, procedures and compliances. The 
Index will facilitate and help organizations to identify areas where they are doing 
well and areas where there is a scope for  improvement. To begin with , 25 Public 
Organizations have been selected from different sectors for assessment. The 
responsibility to conceptualize, study and develop a framework for Integrity Index 
was given to IIM Ahmedabad. Based on the data provided by the selected 
organizations, IIM –Ahmedabad has finalised the pilot project and submitted the 
final report to the CVC which is under examination. The report also contains the 
way forward for further expansion of the project.  
 
(v)    Filling of CVOs posts in CPSEs: 
The posts of CVO, which are full -time, are filled through DoPT. Appointments of 
CVOs in 113 CPSEs are processed through DoPT. There are some PSUs, which are 
smaller in size including newly set up PSUs, wherein full time CVOs are not yet in 
place and i t is for the administrative Ministries concerned to take appropriate steps 
for creating posts of CVOs and filling them up. 

10 
 
Regarding filling up of vacant posts, a common online application form for Central 
Staffing Scheme and CVOs has been introduced making it easier for officers to 
apply. Cadre Controlling Authorities of All India Services and Organized Group -A 
Services are b eing addressed from time to time to nominate officers for Central 
Deputation.  
(vi) On Whistle-blowers policy: 
The Whistle-blowers Protection Act, 2011 (17 of 2014) is yet to come into force. At 
present, the Commission is discharging its functions under the pro visions of Public 
Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers Resolution, 2004 (PIDPI) and 
subsequent amendment made in 2013. Para 6, 7and 7A of PIDPI Resolution 
authorises the Commission, the designated agency, to take such action as deemed fit 
or give suitable directions to the concerned public servant or the public authority if a 
Whistle-blower aggrieved of victimisation or a witness requiring protection, makes 
an application in this regard or the designated authority forwards the same. 
Various Publi c-Sector Organisations have also introduced internal Whistle -blower 
mechanism in their organisations which are functional.  So far, the Commission has 
not faced any impediments in implementation of the PIDPI Resolution. The CVC 
had also taken up the matter with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to provide 
security cover to the genuine Whistle -blowers. In this regard, MHA had taken up 
the issue with State Governments for necessary requirement.  
Findings of the Committee: 
Focus on Preventive Vigilance 
2.13 During interaction with managements of certain PSUs during Study Visit and CVC in 
Delhi, the Committee was apprised that the focus has shifted from punitive to preventive 
vigilance. Certain measures are in place for internal surveillance to check misconduc t of 
employees within the organization. During the visit representatives of various PSUs/PSBs 
informed the Committee that online tendering, bill tracking, e -procurement, e -auction, 
online filing and tracking of complaints, online grievance reporting and redressal mechanism 
etc. are carried out under preventive vigilance administration. The Committee feels that the 
possibility of involving employees associations and trade unions in strengthening 
preventive vigilance should also be explored.  
2.14 The Committ ee notes that CVC in its report ‘TOP 100 BANKING FRAUDS’ 
presented a sector-wise analysis of frauds and their general modus operandi, loopholes 
in the existing system and suggested systemic improvements to plug them. The 
Committee impresses upon the Ministries concerned to ensure that organizations 
under their jurisdiction carry out systemic improvements suggested by the 
Commission and strengthen fraud prevention mechanism to reduce the incidence of 
frauds. 
Integrity Pact 
2.15 Integrity Pact is a tool of preventive vigilance administration, which is enforced since 
December, 2007 and involves the signing of a pact between the procuring organisation and 
the bidders that they will not indulge in corrupt practices in the tendering, award and the 
execution of the contract. Public procurement being the government activity most vulnerable 
to corruption has been a priority concern of the Commission.  Integrity Pact is intended to 

11 
 
make public procurement transparent by binding both parties to ethical conduct. IP  covers 
all activities related to the contract from pre -selection of bidders, bidding and contracting, 
implementation, completion and operation. 
2.16 The Committee appreciates the constant endeavour of Central Vigilance 
Commission to bring in transparency,  equity and competitiveness in procurement and 
contracting through promoting the adoption and implementation of integrity pact. The 
Committee notes that multiple benefits like improved transparency, image and 
reputation as an ethical organization;  reduced external interference, frivolous lawsuits 
and complaints from vendors;  speed up the Tenders Procurement Process; etc.  have 
been accrued to ONGC, which is the first organization in In dia to implement Integrity 
Pact. The Committee therefore recommends that I ntegrity Pact is implemented in all 
government agencies/organization and it is strengthened as a tool of robust preventive 
vigilance mechanism.  
Integrity Index 
2.17 Integrity Index is an extension of Integrity Pact. The Central Vigilance Commission 
had un dertaken an initiative to develop an Integrity Index applicable to a wide range of 
Public Sector and Government Organizations. The development of the Integrity Index is in 
line with the CVC’s broader strategy and emphasis on preventive measures. This is an  
exercise by the organizations for self -assessment of its policies, procedures and 
compliances. The Index will facilitate and help organizations to identify areas where they 
are doing well and areas where there is a scope for improvement.  
2.18 To begin with 25 Public Organizations have been selected from different sectors for 
the assessment. The responsibility to conceptualize, study and develop a framework for 
Integrity Index has been given to IIM Ahm edabad. Based on the data provided by the 
selected organizations, IIM –Ahmedabad has finalised the pilot project and submitted the 
final report to the CVC which is under examination.  The Committee hopes that Integrity 
Index is progressively extended  to cover all G overnment organizations and it is 
implemented in a manner that it promotes a healthy competition among the 
organisations to climb up the ladder. 
Training of Vigilance Officers 
2.19 During interaction with the CMDs/CVOs of various PSUs/PSBs , a need was felt for 
the enhancement of training provisions for Vigilance Officers. CVOs and Vigilance Officers  
have neither exposure nor experience in the field of vigilance at the time of their 
appointment, thus there is a need to thoroughly train them on various aspects of vigilance 
administration. T he current training arrangements available to them have proved to be 
inadequate. Especially with the advancement of technology, the incidences of frauds and 
other areas of vulnerability have increased considerably.  
2.20 In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is a dire need to revamp the 
current training apparatus of CVOs and VOs in PSUs/PSBs by promoting awareness 
about latest technologies. The Committee, accordingly, recommends  CVC to prepare 
extensive training framework/modules for CVOs and VOs of PSUs/PSBs by giving due 
regard to their specific areas of operations.  The Committee also recommends CVC to 
revamp the existing training programme so as to enable CVOs and vigilance officials to 
keep pace with changing times with focus on advanced technology and forensics. 

12 
 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) 
2.21 CVC, in their submission before the Committee on the subject  on 1st October, 2018, 
has informed that for strengthening the vigilance system in banks  and to avert systemic 
failures, the Commission has been advocating adopti on of  Standard Operating Procedures 
(SOPs) in various areas of management. To bring down the incidence of mis -judgement, the 
Commission has been advising the  CVO concerned for improving the training provision for 
officials at various levels and also for job rotation from time to time so that officers are 
tuned to work in different areas of operations. To reduce the commercial lapses affecting 
banks and insuran ce companies, the Commission has been advocating strict adherence to 
KYC norms, due diligence, proper monitoring, etc.  
2.22 The Committee is in complete agreement with the views of the Commission, and 
recommends that learning from the abovementioned short  comings diagnosed by the 
commission, proactive steps are taken by PSUs/PSBs to avert recurrence of such 
frauds in future.  The PSUs, PSBs and Insurance Companies should put in place SOPs 
for all their activities, by clearly defining role, function and del egation, at all levels in 
the organization, leaving a minor or no role for use of discretion. 
2.23 The Committee also observes that most scams and financial frauds unearthed in 
the country in recent times are transnational in character and involved round t ripping 
of funds. Round tripping usually involves several layers of financial transactions and a 
maze of companies, banks and foreign investors, thus presenting a formidable 
challenge for the investigators to establish the money trail. In view of rising in cidence 
of transnational crimes, the Committee recommends the investigating agencies to 
create a pool of dedicated investigators with significant expertise in forensic audit.  
Centralised Database of Suspicious Entities  
2.24 The Committee observes that in majority of bank frauds, the borrowers diverted the 
funds by opening current accounts with other banks, which are not members of the 
consortium and which are not lenders of the borrower. The Committee also notes that 
financing and technology based frauds and frauds based on fake identity, fake KYC 
documents, fake financial statements and fake property documents have emerged as bigger 
challenges in the banking sector. Therefore, the Committee is of the considered view that 
a Ce ntralised Database containing details of suspicious entities, fraudsters and their 
general modus operandi be created by collating data available with individual 
organizations, regulators, investigating agencies as seamless sharing of such 
information among all the stakeholders concerned will bring down cases of all nature. 
CSR for Vigilance 
2.25 During the deliberations of the Committee with PSUs, it was observed that pilferage 
of goods at source and during transportation has been a big concern. The Committ ee was 
made to understand that the said pilferage is done in connivance of local officers and with 
the involvement of local people. On inquiry, the management had expressed its helplessness 
and termed these kinds of incidents as  a law and order problem. Bu t the Committee thinks 
that a major cause of pilferage of Coal from the mining site by the local population is their 
abject poverty. A large number of unemployed population at the production site of any PSU 
is not at all a good sign for the growth of that PSU. 

13 
 
2.26 The Committee is of the view that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), 
through which companies give back to the society , has the potential to uplift the living 
standards of the local population. But , usually,  companies spend the amount 
earmarked for CSR activities  towards the development of their local township and 
infrastructure and for the benefit of the employees of the organisation and a very 
insignificant part of it is spent for the development of neighbourhood. The local 
population is by and large, deprived of benefits of CSR activities. The Committee feels 
that once the Company’s CSR funds are streamlined towards the upliftment of local 
population, the activities such as pilferage might come down. 
Incentives for Vigilance Officers 
2.27 During interaction with  PSUs/PSBs, the Committee learned that the y are finding it 
hard to attract and retain talented Vigilance Officers in their organisations. Thus, it has been 
suggested that Vigilance Officers should be provided  with some incentives to work in the 
Vigilance Department. Vigilance Officers are drawn from within the organization and on 
their selection/appointment as Vigilance Officer s they are diverted from their core area of 
work. In the prevailing scenario, the role of Vigilance Offi cers in the organization has 
assumed greater significance and therefore, an organisation requires talented and motivated 
Vigilance Officers for improving effectiveness of Vigilance Administration.  
2.28 DoPT in their written submission has informed that ou t of 36 vacant posts of CVOs, 
31 posts are located outside Delhi, for which only limited number of officers had shown 
interest. As officers are not finding posts of CVO outside of Delhi rewarding enough, the 
posts are laying vacant for want of sufficient a pplications. The Committee , therefore 
recommends that a provision for special allowance may be made for the CVOs, 
especially for those posted outside Delhi to effectively attract and retain talent. 
2.29 Further, the representatives of various bodies brought to the notice of the 
Committee the plight of the officers working in the vigilance department. The 
Committee notes that officers working in Vigilance face delicate situation when they 
return to parent department as they have to work with colleagues against whom they 
handled Vigilance case(s). This may affect their functioning and judgement in 
investigation. Hence, the Committee suggests CVC to ensure that at least 50% of the 
sanctioned strength of vigil ance Department is drawn on deputation from other 
organization as far as practicable. 
Whistle-Blowers Protection Policy 
2.30 The Hon'ble Supreme Court in a Writ Petition (Civil) No. 539/2003 filed after the 
murder of Shri Satyendra Dubey, a whistle-blower, directed that a machinery be put in place 
for acting on complaints from whistle-blowers till a law is enacted. The Law Commission of 
India had in its 179 th report, inter alia, recommended formulation of  a specific legislation 
titled ‘ The public Interest D isclosure (Protection of Informers) Bill, 2002 ’ to encourage 
disclosure of information regarding corruption or mal -administration by public servants and 
to provide protection to such complainants.  
2.31 In pursuance of the directions, the Government of India on 29 th April, 2004 notified 
the Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers Resolution (PIDPI), 2004 which 
gave powers to the Commission to act on complaints from whistle -blowers. As per the 
Resolution, Central Vigilance Commission is the  designated agency and CVOs of the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are the designated authorities (w.e.f. 

14 
 
14.8.2013) to receive and act on the written complaints/disclosure. In 2007, the report of the 
Second Administrative Reforms Commission also recommended that a specific law needs to 
be enacted to protect whistleblowers. Finally, The Whistleblowers protection Bill was 
introduced in the Parliament in 2011 which finally became an Act in 2014. 
2.32 As per extant guidelines, the complainants ar e required to adhere to certain guidelines 
mentioned in the PIDPI resolution to keep their identity secret. For instance, the complaint 
should be forwarded in a sealed envelope and addressed to the Secretary of the Commission. 
Also, the envelope has to be superscribed ‘Complaints under The Public Interest 
Disclosure’. The text of the complaints should also be carefully drafted so as not to give any 
details or clue as to his/her identity. However, the Committee is of the view that there is a 
little awareness  about the procedure of filing complaint under PIDPI Resolution 
among the public. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to raise 
awareness about PIDPI Resolution through massive public outreach campaigns and 
wide publicity in the print, elect ronic media and also in social media which has 
emerged as a powerful participatory medium of communication in recent times. 
2.33 Further, the said Resolution, inter alia, provides for the protection of whistle-blowers 
from harassment, besides keeping the identity of whistleblowers concealed. However, it has 
been felt that persons who report  corruption or wilful misuse of power or wilful misuse of 
discretion which causes demonstrable loss to the Government or commission of a criminal 
offence by a public servant need statutory protection as protection given to them by the said 
Resolution of the Government of India would not suffice. Accordingly, the Whistle Blowers 
Protection Act, 2014 was enacted and was notified on 12th May, 2014.  
2.34 Consequently, it wa s felt that the  Act required amendments aimed at 
safeguarding against disclosures affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security 
of the State, etc., before it is brought into force, the Government  introduced the 
Whistle Blowers Protecti on (Amendment) Bill, 2015 in the Lok Sabha which was 
passed by the Lok Sabha on 13 th May, 2015. The said Bill was transmitted to the Rajya 
Sabha. However, due to dissolution of 16 th Lok Sabha, this amendment Bill needs to be 
re-introduced in the House.  The Committee hopes that the Whistle Blowers Protection 
(Amendment) Bill, 2015 may be introduced in the House without any further delay and 
passed by both the Houses.  
Information Sharing to Curb Fraud  
2.35 During interaction with PSBs, the Committee was informed that multiple financing, 
technology based frauds, frauds based on fake identity, fake KYC documents, fake financial 
statements and fake property documents have become bigger challenges for them. To 
overcome these challenges, the PSBs suggested seamless sharing of information at all levels, 
amongst all stakeholders, viz. Banks, creditors, regulators, investigating agencies, other 
financial institutions etc. Such information sharing may be done on -line, with in -built 
confidentiality and trust, which will help in bringing down cases of all such nature. In order 
to achieve this, the Committee recommends to employ such novel technologies as Block 
Chain technology, Artificial Intelligence etc. to leave miniscule opportunity for misuse 
by unscrupulous elements . The Gove rnment and the CVC should work together with 
the RBI and Banks to overcome such types of frauds by strengthen ing the existing 
system. 
\ 

15 
 
Accountability of Third Party Entities (TPEs) 
2.36 The PSBs apprised the Committee that Banks have to depend upon the certifications 
of Third Party Entities (TPEs), viz. Advocates, Valuers, Chartered Accountants, 
Transporters, and Warehouses for dispensing various credit facilities. In recent times many 
frauds have come to the notice of Banks due to improper certification done by the TPEs and 
the Banks have failed to hold them accountable.  To ensure accountability of TPEs, the 
Committee recommends that a Code of C onduct and a legally enforceable agreement 
should be executed by all these TPEs, so as to bring in better ethics and accountability 
on their part.

Chapter III 
VIGILANCE ADMINISTRATION IN CENTRAL 
GOVERNMENT BODIES 
 
3. The Committee examined the effectiveness of Vigilance administration in Central 
Government bodies namely, Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and Central Board of 
Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).  Chairman, CBDT and Chairman (in-charge), CBIC 
appeared before the Committee in its meeting held on 10th January, 2020. 
Vigilance Set Up in CBDT 
3.1 Chairman, CBDT made a detailed presentation before the Committee on 10th January 
2020 elaborating the vigilance set up in CBDT . He apprised the Committee that CBDT has a 
separate vigilance set up which is headed by the Director General of Income Tax (Vigilance) 
who is also the Chief Vigilance Officer of the organization.  
3.2 He further apprised that a number of initiatives were taken by CBDT to strengthen 
preventive vigilance, some of them are c omputerization of all the pr ocesses related with 
taxation; Computer Aided Selection of Cases for Scrutiny (CASS) system; online issuance of 
certificates for TDS; making assessments faceless, no interaction between the tax payer and 
the tax officials. These initiatives are called E-Assessment and E-Appeal. 
3.3 He also added that o ne Central Inspection Team has been set up in the Vigilance 
Directorate for quick investigation into complaints of serious nature and Vigilance 
Inspections. Further, systems studies are being conducted by Zonal ADGs on critical 
functional areas to identify loopholes and areas vulnerable to corruption and suggest systemic 
improvements. Th e officers posted in sensitive posts are transferred out on a  regular basis. 
Efforts are made to ensure that no officer continues in such posts for more than three years at 
a stretch.  
3.4 The Committee is appreciative of the actions taken by CBDT to improve 
preventive vigilance in the Department particularly in ter ms of elimination of human 
interference and maximum use of technology. The Committee, however, observes that 
overdependence on these technological tools give rise to new forms of corruption which 
do not require in -person interaction such as digital bribery , blackmail on the basis of 
data, unauthorised access to digital information of taxpayers that corrupt tax officials 
may have.  
3.5 The Committee feels that technology may also lead to complexity of official 
procedures and processes  as officials and tax ev aders who understand technology and 
systems may exploit it to their evil design. Lack of digital literacy or technological 
illiteracy also brings in middlemen having technological knowhow to use the 
vulnerabilities of the service seekers to extort bribes.  The Committee, therefore, feels 
that the CBDT should not fall prey to techno utopianism as  technology is merely an 
advanced tool and is not a final solution to eradicate corruption in departments under 
the purview of CBDT and it is not always true that if  human interference is reduced, 
corruption might go down as it is human beings only who operate these technological 
tools who on occasions may turn fallible.  
3.6 The Committee is of the view that corruption is a big challenge in this country 
and it should be dealt with through various mechanisms. A robust vigilance mechanism 

17 
 
should be put in place as the level of corruption increases where surveillance and 
enforcement by public authority is weak. CBDT may consider appointing officers from 
other organisations on deputation in vigilance units of their organisation for a 
particular period as this would ensure relative impartiality of vigilance officers.  
Besides, a service condition may be added in the Departments under purview of CBDT 
that officers who resign or retire from their services may not join private sector.  
3.7 The Committee notes that CBDT has rolled out faceless e-assessment scheme with the 
intention to eliminate personal interaction between a tax payer and tax officers. The replies to 
the tax notices can be prepared and submitted online without visiting the tax office. CBDT 
has now made it mandatory for tax officers to take recourse to e -communications for  all 
limited and complete scrutiny cases. Earlier, the e -assessment was carried by the Assessing 
Officer but now the role of Assessing Officer shall be limited to only imposition of penalty 
,collection and recovery of demand etc,, and assessment shall be c arried out by the National 
e-Assessment Centres. The Committee notes that, historically, personal interaction 
between tax officer and tax payer has been a major avenue for corruption. The 
Committee feels that faceless assessment will minimize opportunities  for corruption by 
eliminating physical interface and person-to-person contact in the scrutiny assessments. 
The Committee appreciates CBDT for making all out efforts to ensure corruption free 
tax administration. 
3.8 The Committee was also informed that there was a very tedious process of refunds in 
the IT Department. The Committee recommends that a time frame should be put in place 
for refunds as it will ease things for assesses and if no refunds are made in the time 
frame, stern action should be taken against officers concerned. 
3.9 The Committee is aware that the officials who are charged with corruption take 
undue longer time in submitting replies against their charge sheets. The Committee is of 
the view that the time frame should be strictly followed in these cases and a clause 
should be added that those who do not reply to their charge sheets in given time frame 
may be considered guilty of charges made.  
3.10 Chairman of CBDT , while making presentation before the Committee briefed about 
the steps take n to ensure punitive vigilance in the organization. He made the following 
submission: - 
 “As far as punitive vigilance is concerned……we carried out a massive 
exercise of examining the antecedents of the officers and officials who were 
not discharging their  duties efficiently and properly.   We had to resort to 
the provisions of Rule 56(j) and we prematurely retired almost 57 officers.  
Out of those 57 officers, 30 officers belonged to Group 'A' service and the 
rest were from Group 'B' and Group 'C' services .  It is not that we are 
concentrating only on the staff or the junior officers.  We are taking a very, 
very comprehensive view of the entire administrative setup within our 
organization…...so that the functions get discharged very efficiently and in 
a manner in which they ought to be discharged.”

3.13 The Committee appreciates the punitive action taken by CBDT to compulsorily 
retire ‘ dead wood ’ from the Department as  corrupt, errant and non - performing 
officials are burden to the organization and the exchequer. The Committee understands 
that this move was in line with Prime Minister’s Independence Day address at the Red 
Fort last year, where he announced that the ‘black sheep’ in the tax administration who 
may have misused their power by harassing honest taxpayers or taking excessive action 
for minor pr ocedural violations will be removed. This action is also in line with the 
objectives of incumbent Government to clean -up the bureaucracy. The Committee 
recommends that more punitive action is required to be done to improve the image of 
CBDT and a massive exercise should be undertaken in this regard.  
Behavioural Ethics 
3.14 Taxpayers are law abiding citizens of this country and sometimes they feel harassed 
or helpless against rude or arbitrary behaviour of officers who treat them as petty criminals . 
They complain mostly about the rudeness in communication, cancellation of appointment 

19 
 
time, passing on accountability to another officer, raids during unusual time, harassment, 
misconduct and high -handedness of officers and staff. A Member of the Committe e during 
the meeting made following submission in regard to behavioral issues:- 
            “I still want to know whenever you have search operations, we keep hearing 
because I represent a broad spectrum of clients also and even friends I come 
to know, you can have a search operation that is your right, nobody can stop 
that because Section 132 gives you that position, but do you adhere to good 
behavioural norms in those search operations?  It is because what I keep 
hearing always is not what I think should happen.  I am not being very 
critical because I always feel assessee is your asset.  It is like, in courts if, 
there were no clients, there would be no need for Judges and lawyers.  But, 
we treat our clients as if we are the bosses and they are the subject s.  The 
same attitude I find with the Tax Department.  You don't treat your assessee 
as if you are there because of him.  This is our colonial hangover which 
continues to govern us whether it is Judiciary and whether it is Government 
Departments.  That is the one point I am making and that is something to do 
with the ethics that the Chairman was talking about; the behavioural ethics.” 
3.15 Another member of the C ommittee was also critical of the misconduct and rude 
behaviour on the part of income tax officials. He made the following submission:- 
              “From the papers which have been circulated to us, we are not able to get 
anything about the treatment to the assesses.  It is about your officials only.  
You have to treat the assesses with great honou r and respect.  That is not 
found in the Income -Tax Department.  Everyone has got dignity.  They 
have to be treated with utmost dignity.  There is a constitutional guarantee.  
But I find that the tax -papers are treated like accused.  Please have a 
slogan or logo saying that the tax-payers are friends.  They are the persons 
who are giving sources to this country.  I know your limitations of raids 
during nights.  You cannot enter a home during night.  But very often we 
find that your officers enter into the r esidence of the tax -payer during 
night.  You know that right to sleep is a Fundamental Right.  The Supreme 
Court has said it in very clear terms.  I want to know what actions have you 
taken against the officials who enter the houses of the tax -papers durin g 
nights.” 
3.16 The Committee appreciates CBDT for making an all -out effort to augment tax 
collection in the country and bring tax evaders into the tax net. The Committee, 
however, feels that the Department should treat assesses as their assets and follow good 
behavioural norms while conducting searches and raids. Tax Departments across the 
world have changed their stance towards taxpayers in terms of dealing with them which 
is to treat them as partners and clients rather than as tax evaders. The Department  
should adopt corporate etiquettes of service industry and transform into a service -
oriented organization. 
3.17 The Committee is of the view that i nstead of high -handed, arrogant and rude 
conduct, the income tax sleuths should be well behaved and deal with  the public with 
efficiency as well as decency as they are clients and partners of the department. Search 
operations during odd hours in night should also be avoided if there are no compelling 
reasons to do so. The department should have a policy of zero t olerance towards rude 
and arrogant conduct on the part of tax officials with taxpayers and for this the officials 

20 
 
should be imparted training in soft skills so that they could be courteous  and polite  
while dealing with taxpayers. The Committee recommends t hat errant officials should 
be penalized if they resort to such actions even after repeated complaints and warnings. 
The need for remedy could not be more urgent.  
3.18 Filing Income Tax returns is a cumbersome process, full of technicalities and 
therefore challenging. Sometimes, due to the complex nature of online forms, errors 
may creep in inadvertently. The Committee feels that law abiding taxpayers should be 
given an opportunity to rectify their returns. 
Misuse of Income Tax Department 
3.19 It is alleged that the Income Tax Department raids on persons considered close to 
opposition parties and such kind of allegations are made against almost all regimes that 
happen to be in power at the Centre. It is often heard and alleged by the opposition partie s 
that the Income Tax Department was politically being  misused as a ‘revengeful’ arm of those 
in power to target political opponents especially during the elections. 
 
3.20 This issue was raised in the meeting of the Committee held on 10 th January 2020. A 
Member of the Committee while raising this issue stated that there was an impression in the 
country that search operations or notices had a political slant. Another Member of the 
Committee opined that the Income Tax officials are just pawns in the hands of those in power 
who act on their behest. He was also of the opinion that a law should be enacted which 
prohibits them from being rewarded with political or bureaucratic offices post retirement.  
 
3.21 The Committee is of the opinion that CBDT should always conduct its work in a 
neutral, non -partisan and non -discriminatory manner so that the Department could 
gain respect in the eyes of the general masses for its political neutrality and no one could 
accuse them of working under political pressures. Working of  enforcement agencies 
under pressureof those in power creates crisis for institutional autonomy and against 
the very spirit of the concept of political neutrality of bureaucracy which may endanger 
the very fundamentals of democracy.

Vigilance Set Up in CBIC 
 
4. Directorate General of Vigilance (DGoV) is the apex body under the Board for 
vigilance administration in CBIC. It is headed by the Principal Director General of Vigilance , 
who functions as the full time CVO of CBIC. DGoV is an attached o ffice of CBIC in the 
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. CBIC has informed that several initiatives have 
been taken to strengthen preventive vigilance in the Board. DGoV undertakes surprise checks 
of sensitive formations through zonal units by assigning minimum number of surprise checks.  
4.1 It has been further informed by CBIC that Zonal Units of DGoV conduct s Vigilance 
Audits of their jurisdictional Commissionerates. During these audits, it is verified whether the 
systems and procedures laid down under various Rules/regulations/notifications etc. are being 
scrupulously followed. In addition to Vigilance Section which deals with the complaints 
against officers, special focus is given to determine the presence of vigilance angle in the 
critical areas like investigation, adjudication, refund, drawback and audit in the 
Commissionerates.  
 
4.2 Vigilance Directorate has been enhanced by creation of three new zones to strengthen 
preventive vigilance and officers under CBIC are being rotated between s ensitive and non -
sensitive posts on a regular basis. The Department of Revenue has appointed an Independent 
External Monitor (IEM) for Department of Revenue, CBIC and CBDT. It has also been 
decided that contracts of procurements of services in excess of Rs .50 lakhs, procurement of 
goods in excess of Rs.1 crore, and construction projects in excess of Rs.50 lakh shall be 
overseen by IEM.  
4.3 CBIC has also informed the Committee about application of  advanced technologies to 
bring in transparency and also to reduce human intervention in the Board. They informed 
about Risk Management System (RMS) technology which ensures clearance of about 85% 
consignments without assessment and examination and now only selected consignments are 
taken up for scrutiny and examination. Further the Indian Customs EDI Gateway (ICEGATE) 
introduced 24x7 e -filing, e-payment, electronic message exchange and helpline & combined 
with the Indian Customs EDI System (ICES), is the engine for effective handling of nearly ten 
million export and import documents annually as also 24x7 clearance of cargo. 
4.4 CBIC further informed about several other online mechanism s instituted  to reduce  
human intervention and also to improve vigilance administration in the Board. Some of them 
are E -SANCHIT, ICE TRAK, E -Payment of Duty, ICEDASH, E -Sealing, Advance 
Passengers Information System (APIS), Direct Port Delivery (DPD) Direct Port Entry (DPE), 
Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT), etc.   
4.5    Regarding preventive vigilance set up in pl ace at ports in the country, the Chairman, 
CBIC in the meeting of the Committee held on 10th January 2020 submitted as under:- 
“almost one crore of containers come into the country.  We are transacting 
almost one crore  of containers but we hardly examine five per cent to ten per 
cent of that because almost seventy per cent to seventy -five per cent of the 
containers coming at any port in the country would go outside without 
examination. We have red flag indicators.  We h ave found out, depending on 
the profile of the party who is importing, where the goods are coming from, 
what type of goods are coming. We have profile based on that one.  We have a 

22 
 
very robust mechanism of red flag in the consignments and we have got a ris k 
management system which automatically gives whether the consignment has to 
be examined or not.  So, what happens is this. When the goods come in, they 
need to be examined unless the system says that it has to be examined.  
To that extent, the interaction or the discretion of the officer concerned would 
be reduced so that he would not be able to make out any mischief out of that 
particular activity which he is holding onto. Further, we have also done 
something called direct p ort delivery.  That means for the ship itself, the 
container would go into a truck or a train and it can be cleared. I mean there is 
no human intervention in that one.  Similarly, on export side also, we are 
giving something like direct port export but whe n these additional facilities are 
being given, we need to control that some bad elements do not bring goods into 
the country which are not supposed to come into the country without payment 
of duty or goods which can create a problem for the security of the  country.  
For that, we have been installing scanners across the country.  Across the 
major ports, we have installed scanners which also get scanned.  That scanner 
library is also being consulted by the officer in -charge so without a human 
intervention per se in the field we are able to control the way the goods are 
moving in.” 
4.6 The Committee takes note of the submission of CBIC in regard to the steps taken 
to strengthen preventive vigilance in the Department as well as at ports, airports etc. 
through ma ximum use of advance technology and reducing human intervention. The 
Committee appreciates that the CBIC has taken various measures such as ICEGATE, 
E-SANCHIT, ICETRAK, E -Payment of Duty, APIS, DPE, SWIFT etc. to streamline 
fast movement of goods and servi ces and to ensure robust preventive mechanism in the 
organisation.  
4.7 The Committee also notes that there are scanning and examination facilities at 
ports of our country in which only 5-10 per cent of the total containers per consignment 
are scanned and are picked up randomly by the system for scanning as ports have 
limited capacities for scanning. The Committee recommends that full -body or drive -
through scanners should be installed in a phased manner at all the ports in such a way 
that trucks or other vehicles carrying containers can simply pass through these scanners 
and get fully scanned as has been done at some integrated check posts and ports in the 
country. This will ensure 100 per cent scanning.  The Committee believes that after 
installation of the full body or drive through scanners at all the ports, the smuggling of 
concealed drugs, weapons and other contraband through the ports will be curbed. This 
will put an end to smuggling and subsequent revenue losses and criminal and terrorist 
activities.  
4.8 The Committee is also aware of the limitations of  scanners as they are manned 
by fallible officials who may fall prey to bribery as had happened during Mumbai bomb 
blast of 1993 in which some customs officials including an IRS officer had aided and 
abetted illegal imports of RDX and other weapons for the Mumbai bomb blast. In view 
of this, the Committee recommends that a f ool proof vigilance set up should be put in 
place and stern actions should be taken action corrupt officials in a time bound manner 
as the involvement of corrupt officials in import or export of illegal items may not only 
cause revenue loss but also pose threat to national security. The Committee also 

23 
 
recommends that CBIC may also appoint officers on deputation from other 
organisations in their vigilance units as they , being outsiders, may act in non -partisan 
manner during their limited tenure.
