CHAPTER-III 
 
BENEFITS OF VIRTUAL COURTS AND WAY FORWARD 
 
3.1 Despite shortcomings, Virtual Courts have infinite benefits to offer for all the 
stakeholders involved. Moving to a largely virtual system has long term benefits for the 
judiciary, advocates and the public at large. 
Management of Docket explosion 
3.2 The Committee notes that India has been experiencing Docket explosion and Courts 
are staring at an avalanche of cases. At present, more than 30 million cases are pending in 
different Courts across the country. The problem of huge arrears of pending cases has be en 
retarding the efficiency of justice dispensation system and the rights of citizens to timely 
delivery of Justice. 
3.3 Inspite of various attempts such as reforms in Procedural Laws, tribunalisation, 
adoption of Alternative Dispute Resolution mechanism, establishment of Fast Track Courts 
and constitution of Courts under different statutes, the reduction of arrears in Courts and 
ensuring timely Justice to the litigant public continue to be a major challenge to the Indian 
Judiciary. 
3.4 The Committee believ es that ‘Justice delayed is Justice denied’ but ‘Justice 
hurried is also Justice buried’. The Committee is of the view that Virtual Courts is a 
mechanism that will strike a balance between these two extremes and extends 
expeditious Justice to the litigant public without compromising quality . The Committee 
feels that transfer of certain categories of cases from regular Court establishments to 
Virtual Courts will reduce the pendency of cases which has been clogging the wheels of 
Justice for decades. 
3.5 To continue with the functioning of Virtual Courts in all the Courts even during 
non pandemic time, the Committee feels that the present system should be allowed to 
continue on an experimental basis with the consent of all parties for certain categories of 
cases like Appeals etc  and final hearings where physical presence of the parties/counsels 
is not required and online virtual hearing alone is sufficient. The expenditure involved in 
the establishment of a large number of Tribunals /Courts can be cut down size ably. This 
will also reduce the crowd in the court and cut down other litigation costs and 
overheads. 
 
3.6 The Committee is also of the opinion that Virtual Courts can be extended 
permanently to various Appellate Tribunals like TDSAT, IPAB, NCLAT etc., loc ated 
across the country which do not require personal appearances of the parties/advocates. 
Permanent Virtual Courts can also be established for hearing matters relating to 
Administrative and other Tribunals at the time of final hearing. This will cut down  the 
cost and increase the efficiency in disposal of the cases without being unnecessarily being 
adjourned. The Committee is also of the opinion that necessary Amendments may be 
brought in laws to legalise Virtual Courts and its proceedings without being 
unnecessarily challenged before Courts. 
Promotes Docket Inclusion 

22 
 
3.7 The Committee notes that still in some parts of the country a substantial number of 
people have limited access to Justice and are unable to approach Courts due to locational or 
economic handicaps. 
3.8 The Committee notes that India's Courts are organised based on pecuniary thresholds 
when it comes to civil matters and gravity thresholds (how grave the crime is) when it comes 
to criminal matters. This means, that more often than not, there  is only one principal District 
Court for a whole district. In large states, some districts can be as large as some countries. 
Parties have to travel quite far to ensure that they can access the Court  premises. Further, not 
just parties, their lawyers also  must travel far to access Courts. On the appellate side of most 
High Courts, parties, and counsel, travel all the way from the districts to attend hearings. 
3.9 The Committee believes that Virtual Courts can better promote the principle of 
Distributive Ju stice. Distributive Justice requires that Court services should be 
accessible to all and that the service should be affordable by all. No member of the 
general public should be disadvantaged by locational or economic handicaps or 
otherwise. The Committee i s of the opinion that Digital Justice is cheaper and faster. 
People living in remote and far flung areas can also take part in Court proceedings 
through videoconferencing without having to spend a fortune to set foot in the 
Courtroom. 
Access to Justice 
3.10  The Committee notes that Goal 16 of the Sustainable Development Goals framework 
is dedicated to the promotion of peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, 
the provision of access to justice for all, and building accountable instituti ons at all levels. 
Target 16.3  ‘Promote the rule of law at the national and international levels and ensure 
equal access to justice for all’ is to be achieved by 2030.The Committee hopes that Virtual 
Courts will help India accelerate progress towards achieving its SDG target 16.3by 2030. 
3.11 Access to Justice is a Fundamental Right. Virtual Court system can increase access to 
justice by addressing locational and economic handicaps. For instance, people from remote 
and far flung areas can access the Su preme Court through a competent lawyer without having 
to spend a fortune in travelling all the way to the National Capital time and again. 
3.12    Videoconferencing facilitates a lawyer to argue in any Court in any part of India. Cases 
can be heard from se veral Courts in a single day. A lawyer can argue in one Court in the 
morning, and be present for a case in another Court later in the day. This is not possible with 
physical Court hearings.  Thus, both advocates and litigants have wider choice and this will  
result in substantial reduction of costs associated with litigation in appellate Courts which may 
otherwise require instructing a local lawyer. Litigants need not leave their work to attend 
Court as they can access proceedings from their home or office. V irtual proceedings also 
mitigate significant logistical costs incurred in the transportation of prisoners between jail and 
Court. 
3.13 Virtual Courts also enable vulnerable witnesses to provide testimony from a safer 
environment. Also, Virtual hearings are  more convenient and less traumatic for children, 
women and victims of abuse and the differently abled who cannot easily attend physical 
hearings in Courtrooms. 
3.14 The Committee also feels that at present, there is an enormous gulf between 
knowing one’s rights and being able to enforce them. Only well resourced 

23 
 
individuals/organizations are able to deploy lawyers and fight for justice. Virtual Courts 
have the potential to bridge the gap between people knowing the law and being able to 
enforce their entitlements, thereby creating a level playing field between the affluent and 
the less well off, between those who have always had Courts at their disposal and those 
who have always felt alienated. In the opinion of the Committee, Virtual Courts deliver 
‘Enforceable Justice’.   
Speedy Justice 
3.15    The Committee notes that one of the principal benefits of Virtual Courts is that they 
expedite processes and procedures which would otherwise be protracted and laborious. 
Virtual Courts can deliver results faster and  with fewer resources. Virtual Courts also reduce 
commute time to the Courts and wait time at the Courts. Dedicated time slots will in still more 
disciplined time management. 
3.16 Virtual Courts helps in concise, pointed and focused arguing by lawyers maki ng the 
system faster. Drawing a comparison between Virtual Court hearings and regular Court 
hearings, the Secretary, Department of Justice said, 
 ‘Videoconferencing has led to a change in style and approach before the 
Court. Now, you have to go in for very concise oral arguments. You don’t have 
time to carry on arguments for a very long time. There is also a change in the 
manner in which you handle  witnesses and adversaries. That also has changed 
quite a bit as compared to an open Court where the entire spirit and ethos are a 
little different.’ 
3.17 Also, the problem of truncated hearings interspersed by frequent adjournments can be 
avoided as there  can be no excuse for litigants and lawyers not being able to attend Court. 
Repeated adjournment of cases, truncated hearings are resulting in rescheduling Court process 
and disrupting the progress of the case. 
3.18 The Committee is of the opinion that int roduction of Virtual Courts would result 
in an improvement over traditional Courts as they are more affordable, citizen friendly 
and offers greater access to justice. They yield substantial savings in costs for both 
individual litigants and Courts. Traditi onal Courts, by and large, are accessible to very 
few people and even then only at disproportionate expense and effort, Virtual Courts 
can help overcome these injustices. 
 
 
Proportionate Justice 
3.19 The Committee feels that the Court system is already bog ged down by arrears. The 
Committee notes that at present there is no mechanism to segregate simple cases which can be 
disposed of within shortest possible time as compared to complex cases involving 
cumbersome procedures and number of witnesses. Petty case s which constitute a major chunk 
of the caseload need to be separated from complex ones.  
3.20 In the opinion of the Committee, Virtual Courts can better promote the principle 
of Proportionate Justice. The principle of Proportionate Justice requires that t he 
expense, speed, complexity and the extent of combativeness of any case should be 
proportionate to the substance and scale of that case. The Committee feels that there 
should be some mechanism to segregate simple cases from complex ones .In simple 

24 
 
terms, one should not use a sledge hammer to crack a nut. Petty cases should be dealt 
with swiftly in a reasonable timeframe. Such cases should not require cumbersome 
procedures. 
Pilot project and the way forward 
3.21 The representatives of the Bar contended tha t Virtual Courts do injustice to the art of 
advocacy as they deprive the advocates of an opportunity to argue and put forth one’s case 
and change the course of arguments based on the changing dynamics of a case during the 
hearing. Most lawyers find it diff icult to present their case efficiently and effectively via 
videoconferencing. 
3.22They further submitted that an advocate gets to understand the mood of the judges and 
stands a better chance at convincing them during physical hearings. However, online 
hearing creates a psychological pressure on both the advocates as well as the judges. 
Physical presence can serve important expressive functions, particularly during cross -
examination, which ultimately leads to the discovery of truth. Evidence recorded by mea ns of 
video conferencing may distort non -verbal cues such as facial expressions, postures, and 
gestures. For instance, delayed streaming may come in the way of detecting facial reactions. 
Even in a live stream that is working perfectly, merely the face of a person may 
overemphasize facial expression while leaving gestures partially obscured or out of view 
entirely.  
3.23    The Coordination and cooperation between the briefing counsel and the arguing 
counsel is completely lost in virtual hearings which actually works to the detriment of the 
litigant besides leading to lengthier arguments. Moreover, cases which require intensi ve and 
elaborate hearing on facts and points of law cannot be effectively heard and disposed of by 
Virtual Courts. An inability to cross -examine properly inadvertently increases the risk of 
error. A representative of the Bar said, 
 ‘….That integrity portion or that element of honesty and transparency is 
totally lost. I do not know who all are sitting next to the witness or to the 
opposite side. My screen is basically limited to his camera and whatever his 
webcam can see is all that I can see. I really do not know whether he is under 
duress; he is under coercion or he is being tutored’ 
3.24   They further opined that holding of trials through videoconferencing would have 
several pitfalls and could be a tool for misuse in the hands of unscrupulous litiga nts. The 
whole purpose of judicial tools such as cross examination would be defeated. The trial 
through videoconferencing would encourage witness tutoring and prompting. It would be 
extremely tough to confront witnesses over Video conferencing.  
 
3.25   Speaking on the shortcomings of Virtual Court hearings, a representative of the Bar 
said, 
‘In some cases, there are hundreds of documents which are filed and 
referring to those documents is very difficult. The Judge, who is hearing the 
matter, sometimes ha s a hard copy of the file before him. In many cases, they 
don’t have it. They simply have the pleadings before them. They don’t have 
the documents before them. They don’t have the evidence recorded in the 

25 
 
matter before them. So, how do we address a matter before the Virtual 
Court? In the absence of complete pleadings, complete documents and 
evidence before the Judge, how can we argue? It is not a system which is 
working genuinely and realistically. There is a lot of scope for 
improvement’.  
3.26  The Committ ee is of the view that  digital transformation of the Judiciary has 
important implications for clearing the significant backlog of cases which the 
judiciary is burdened with. Technology may, in fact, be a catalyst for simplifying 
processes and making manual  processes redundant. It will make justice accessible 
and affordable to a large section of the population and help in overcoming physical 
and logistical barriers which prevent many litigants from seeking justice . 
3.27     Virtualized proceedings overcome distance, logistics, delays and costs that currently 
bedevil the Court systems world over. Recently, Justice Chandrachud stated that Virtual 
Courts launched to settle Traffic Challan cases collected 101.74 crores till date, all that 
without the parties having to assemble in the traditional brick and mortar Courtroom. Despite 
infrastructure bottlenecks, over 15 lakh hearings were conducted over videoconferencing 
during the lockdown period. 
3.28 The Committee fully understands that Virtual Courts have their o wn 
shortcomings, however they constitute an advancement over the existing system, and 
therefore, on the overall, they are worth embracing. These current shortcomings might 
be overcome through existing and emerging technologies. Periodical interaction of ba r 
and bench with the technical persons by establishing committees in each 
Courts/Tribunal will help sort out the grievances relating to Virtual Courts and other  
issues then and there. 
3.29 The Committee is of the opinion that a full fledged Virtual Court should be 
piloted in the first instance. This allows the system to be tested in practice which can 
then refined in the light of the feedback received from different stakeholders. It also 
enables the judiciary to identify the type of cases best suited to Virtual Courts. 
3.30 The Committee also recommends Ministry of Electronics and Information 
Technology to employ globally tried and tested tools such as Immersive tele presence 
technology, augmented reality systems to make virtual hearings more lifelike and 
engaging.  
Integration of Virtual Courts into the Legal Ecosystem. 
3.31 Information and Communication technologies have impacted every facet of human 
life. Global legal systems are increasingly embracing evolving technologies to keep pace with 
the information society. It is time, the Court room which is often regarded as the last bastion 
of antiquated working practices opens its doors to latest technology. Multiple factors such as 
constantly increasing case load, huge pendency of cases, resource constraints, need to improve 
access to justice, need to improve efficiency and effectiveness of Court proceedings, 
increasing demand for transparency and accountability and greater expectations on the ability 
to access information and transact with the Court remotely make a case for Virtual Courts in 
India. 
3.32 In 19 th Century, Justice Benjamin Cardoso said, “New times demand new 
measures and new men” in the field of law or elsewhere. This statement is very much 
relevant to the current situation. The Committee is of the considered opinion that 

26 
 
traditional Courtrooms may well remain necessary for our future, but they are certainly 
not sufficient. There is a need to integrate Virtual Courts into the country’s legal 
ecosystem. 
3.33 To begin with, Judiciary may identify categories of cases that can be tried by 
Virtual Courts. Department of Justice in its written replies to the Committee submitted 
that the following cases may be tried in the Virtual Court -Offences under Motor 
Vehicles Act (Traffic Challan cases), Petty offences where summons can be issued under 
Section 206 of CrPC., Cases registered under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 
Motor Accident Claim Petition cases. The Committee is of the view that all such matters 
where personal presence may be dispensed with, can be transferred from regular Court 
establishments to Virtual Courts. The Committee believes that Virtual adjudication will 
bring massive benefits across the system.  
3.34 In respect of complex cases such as those involving interpretation of Law, facts, 
examination of a large number of witnesses and s o forth, a hybrid model may be 
adopted wherein manual processes such as filing of plaint, vakalatnama, issuing of 
summons etc.. may be automated and digitized and the hearing may be held in a 
physical Courtroom. 
3.35 Since integration of Virtual courts int o the legal ecosystem will have a significant 
impact on all stakeholders, the Committee feels that Members of Bar Associations and 
Bar councils must also be involved in evolving a consensual process. This would avoid 
unnecessary opposition and irritants. 
3.36 The facility of Virtual Courts extended to lawyers should also be considered for 
extension to private litigants who appear in person or have to travel to High Courts from 
different states and cities and places. This would go a long way in strengthening  public 
confidence and improving  perception about the reachability of the judicial system. 
3.37 The concept of Virtual Courts has gained immense ground during COVID -19 
Pandemic times. It is and will remain the new reality and the new normal. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the concept of Virtual Courts may well be 
extended to cover arbitration hearings, conciliation and Summary trials. For instance, if 
national and international arbitrations are allowed to be conducted through  Virtual 
Courts , there will be hardly any requirement for real time travel to distant locations. 
The Committee believes that this move will unlock the Courts and also mitigate the 
inconvenience of attending Courts as long distance travels can be dispensed with and 
proceedings become less expensive as well.

CHAPTER-II 
CHALLENGES OF VIRTUAL COURTS 
1. Department of Justice in its written replies to the Committee submitted that  
E-Seva kendras have been established in all the High Courts and in one District 
Court in each state as a part of a pilot project to provide assistance to lawyers and 
litigants ranging from information to facilitation and e filing. The Committee is 
highly ap preciative of this initiative and believes that E-Seva Kendras will go a 
long way in bridging the ‘access divide’ and hopes that such facilitation centres be 
set up in all Court complexes across the country at the earliest. The Committee 
recommends that th e feasibility of involving private agencies/service providers 
who can help people who are not tech savvy in connecting with Courts by taking 
VC equipment to their door steps on payment may be explored.    (Para 2.7) 
 
2. As regards connectivity divide, the Committee recommends the Ministry of 
communications to step up efforts to ensure timely implementation of National 
Broadband mission which envisages broadband access to all so that the services 
provided by indigenous com munication satellites are fully harnessed and the goal 
of Universal broadband access is achieved.       (Para 2.9) 
 
3. The Committee is of the opinion that the Judiciary may also consider such 
innovative solutions as launching mobile videoconferencing facilit ies for the 
benefit of advocates and people living in remote areas.              (Para 2.10) 
 
4. The Committee is of the view that with the advent of Information technology, 
there is not a single facet of human life that is left untouched by it. ICT has also 
transformed the legal landscape in India and the Indian judiciary has come a long 
way from a paper-based era to the one dominated by digital technology and is now 
moving towards cloud based technology. The Committee believes that in coming 
times, technology will emerge as a game changer and advocates would be required 
to use technological skills in combination with their specialized legal knowledge 
and therefore, they should keep up with the changing times.             (Para 2.13)

computer course as one of the subjects in three year/five year courses to enable the

systems while they pursue the Law Course. This will help educate and equip 
budding lawyers with knowledge and skills required for handling digital 
platforms.          (Para2.17)

to continue on an experimental basis with the consent of all parties for certain 
categories of cases like Appeals etc and final hearings w here physical presence of 
the parties/counsels is not required and online virtual hearing alone is sufficient. 
The expenditure involved in the establishment of a large number of Tribunals 
/Courts can be cut down sizeably. This will also reduce the crowd in  the court and 
cut down other litigation costs and overheads.        (Para3.5) 
 
20. The Committee is also of the opinion that Virtual Courts can be extended 
permanently to various Appellate Tribunals like TDSAT, IPAB, NCLAT etc., 
located across the country whi ch do not require personal appearances of the 
parties/advocates. Permanent Virtual Courts can also be established for hearing 
matters relating to Administrative and other Tribunals at the time of final hearing. 
This will cut down the cost and increase the efficiency in disposal of the cases 
without being unnecessarily being adjourned. The Committee is also of the opinion 
that necessary Amendments may be brought in laws to legalise Virtual Courts and 
its proceedings without being unnecessarily challenged before Courts. 
                                                                                                                              (Para3.6) 
 
21. The Committee believes that Virtual Courts can better promote the principle of 
Distributive Justice. Distributive Justice requires that Court services should be 
accessible to all and that the service should be affordable by all. No member of the 
general pu blic should be disadvantaged by locational or economic handicaps or 
otherwise. The Committee is of the opinion that Digital Justice is cheaper and 
faster. People living in remote and far flung areas can also take part in Court 
proceedings through videoconf erencing without having to spend a fortune to set 
foot in the Courtroom.           (Para3.9) 
 
22. The Committee also feels that at present, there is an enormous gulf between 
knowing one’s rights and being able to enforce them. Only well resourced 
individuals/organizations are able to deploy lawyers and fight for justice. Virtual 
Courts have the potenti al to bridge the gap between people knowing the law and 
being able to enforce their entitlements, thereby creating a level playing field 
between the affluent and the less well off, between those who have always had 
Courts at their disposal and those who ha ve always felt alienated. In the opinion of 
the Committee, Virtual Courts deliver ‘Enforceable Justice’.     (Para3.14) 
 
23. The Committee is of the opinion that introduction of Virtual Courts would result in 
an improvement over traditional Courts as they are more affordable, citizen 
friendly and offers greater access to justice. They yield substantial savings in costs 
for both individual litigants and Courts. Traditional Courts, by and large, are 
accessible to very few people and even then only at disproportio nate expense and 
effort, Virtual Courts can help overcome these injustices.     (Para3.18) 
 

31 
 
24. In the opinion of the Committee, Virtual Courts can better promote the principle of 
Proportionate Justice. The principle of Proportionate Justice requires that the 
expense, speed, complexity and the extent of combativeness of any case should be 
proportionate to the substance and scale of that case. The Committee feels that 
there should be some mechanism to segregate simple cases from complex ones .In 
simple terms, on e should not use a sledge hammer to crack a nut. Petty cases 
should be dealt with swiftly in a reasonable timeframe. Such cases should not 
require cumbersome procedures.        (Para3.20) 
 
25. The Committee is of the view that  digital transformation of the Jud iciary has 
important implications for clearing the significant backlog of cases which the 
judiciary is burdened with. Technology may, in fact, be a catalyst for 
simplifying processes and making manual processes redundant. It will make 
justice accessible an d affordable to a large section of the population and help in 
overcoming physical and logistical barriers which prevent many litigants from 
seeking justice .          (Para3.26) 
 
26. The Committee fully understands that Virtual Courts have their own 
shortcomings, however they constitute an advancement over the existing system, 
and therefore, on the overall, they are worth embracing. These current 
shortcomings might be overcome through existing and emerging technologies. 
Periodical interaction of bar and bench with the technical persons by establishing 
committees in each Courts/Tribunal will help sort out the grievances relating to 
Virtual Courts and other  issues then and there.     (Para3.28) 
 
27. The Committee is of the opinion that a full fledged Virtual Court should be piloted 
in the first instance. This allows the system to be tested in practice which can then 
refined in the light of the feedback received from different stakeholders. It  also 
enables the judiciary to identify the type of cases best suited to Virtual Courts.  
             (Para3.29) 
 
28. The Committee also recommends Ministry of Electronics and Information 
Technology to employ globally tried and tested tools such as Immersive tele 
presence technology, augmented reality systems to make virtual hearings more 
lifelike and engaging.         (Para3.30) 
 
29. In 19th Century, Justice Benjamin Cardoso said, “New times demand new measures 
and new men” in the field of law or elsewhere. This statement is very much 
relevant to the current situation. The Committee is of the considered opinion that 
traditional Courtrooms may  well remain necessary for our future, but they are 
certainly not sufficient. There is a need to integrate Virtual Courts into the 
country’s legal ecosystem.          (Para3.32) 
 
30. To begin with, Judiciary may identify categories of cases that can be tried b y 
Virtual Courts. Department of Justice in its written replies to the Committee 
submitted that the following cases may be tried in the Virtual Court -Offences 
under Motor Vehicles Act (Traffic Challan cases), Petty offences where summons 
can be issued under  Section 206 of CrPC., Cases registered under Section 138 of 
Negotiable Instruments Act, Motor Accident Claim Petition cases. The Committee 
is of the view that all such matters where personal presence may be dispensed with, 

32 
 
can be transferred from regular Court establishments to Virtual Courts. The 
Committee believes that Virtual adjudication will bring massive benefits across the 
system.            (Para3.33) 
 
31. In respect of complex cases such as those involving interpretation of Law, facts, 
examination of a large number of witnesses and so forth, a hybrid model may be 
adopted wherein manual processes such as filing of plaint, vakalatnama, issuing of 
summons etc.. may be automated and digitized and the hearing may be held in a 
physical Courtroom.          (Para3.34) 
 
32. Since integration of Virtual courts into the legal ecosystem will have a significant 
impact on all stakeholders, the Committee feels that Members of Bar Associations 
and Bar councils must also be involved in evolving a consensual process. This 
would avoid unnecessary opposition and irritants.      (Para3.35) 
 
33. The facility of Virtual Courts extended to lawyers should also be considered for 
extension to private litigants who appear in person or have to travel to High Courts 
from different states a nd cities and places. This would go a long way in 
strengthening public confidence and improving perception about the reachability 
of the judicial system.          (Para3.36) 
 
34. The concept of Virtual Courts has gained immense ground during COVID -19 
Pandemic times. It is and will remain the new reality and the new normal. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the concept of Virtual Courts may well be 
extended to cover arbitrat ion hearings, conciliation and Summary trials. For 
instance, if national and international arbitrations are allowed to be conducted 
through Virtual Courts, there will be hardly any requirement for real time travel 
to distant locations. The Committee believ es that this move will unlock the Courts 
and also mitigate the inconvenience of attending Courts as long distance travels can 
be dispensed with and proceedings become less expensive as well.   (Para3.37)

R E P O R T 
  
 This Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on the recommendations/observations 
of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public 
Grievances, Law and Justice in its One Hundredth Report on the Demands for Grants (2020 -
21) of the Ministry, which was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok 
Sabha on the 6th March, 2020. 
2. The Committee had made as many as 4 6 recommendations/observations in its One 
Hundredth Report. Replies of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions  
thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under three chapters on the basis of satisfaction 
of the Committee. Out of 46 rec ommendations where final replies have been received as 
many as 34 (74 percent approximately) of total recommendations are satisfactory.  These 
replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations (17) which have been accepted  by the 
Ministry, i.e. in respect of paras 2.18, 2.72, 3.2, 3.10, 3.19, 3.25, 4.3, 5.2, 
5.14, 5.15, 6.20, 6.25, 7.7, 7.15, 8.12, 8.15 and 8.18  of the Report. The 
Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted those 
recommendations. 
Chapter – II:  Recommendations/observations (17) which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies given by the Ministry, i.e. in respect of paras 
2.7, 2.40, 2.43, 3.13, 3.27, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 5.3, 5.12, 6.9, 6.21, 6.27, 6.31, 7.9, 
8.6 and 8.10  of th e Report. The Committee is satisfied with the 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue those 
as of now.  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations (12) in respect of which Committee has 
not accepted the replies of the Ministry, i.e. with regard to paras 2.21, 3.6, 
3.16, 3.22, 4.4, 5.9, 5.13, 6.5, 6.7, 6.13, 6.18 and 7.12  of the Report. The 
Committee does not accept the reasons given for not accepting its 
recommendations of the Committee and reiterates the same. 
3. The Committee d esires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the 
Committee in this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in t he 
succeeding pages.

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY: 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.0 The Ministry is implementing only two schemes - i) Training Schemes;   ii) 
Administrative Reforms and Pensioners’ Schemes. An allocation of 194.27 crore was made 
for the Schemes in BE2019 -20 which was reduced to 168.43 crore at RE stage. The Ministry 
has been able to spend only 94.98 crore i.e. just 56.39%  of the funds till 31st January, 2019. 
The Committee expresses its concern over the pattern of expenditure and recommends the 
Ministry to take corrective measures for proportionate and timely disbursement of funds. It is 
also observed that the outlay provi ded for the Schemes in BE 2020 -21 is 4.27 crore less than 
the allocation made in BE 2019 -20. The Committee recommends that all possible efforts be 
made by the Ministry to devise more Schemes aimed at capacity building, strengthening 
human resource potentia l, reforming administration and improving governance. The 
Committee strongly feels that there is a need for boisterous Government support to such 
schemes.                    (Para 2.18) 
Action Taken 
1.1 RE 2019 -20 allocations were in tune with the requirem ents of funds for the two 
Training schemes in the previous financial year.   The concern of the Department Related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee shown on the slow pace of utilization of funds in FY 
2019-20 has been noted and will be taken care of for ne cessary compliance in future. BE 
2020-21 allocations of Rs 190.00 Crore in respect of the two schemes of the Ministry seems 
adequate at this point, however any additional requirement of funds would be taken up with 
M/o Finance at appropriate stages in the financial year.   
1.2 As regards the Committee’s recommendation to make all possible efforts to devise 
more Schemes aimed at capacity building, strengthening human resource potential, reforming 
administration and improving governance, it is informed that a n Integrated Government 
Online Training (iGOT) programme has been launched in December, 2018 to augment the 
existing training mechanism with on -line module based training coupled with certification 
with the objective of making training inputs available to Government officers /officials on -
sight and on-flexi time basis.  
1.3 In this sequence, a new version of iGOT (iGOT 2.0) is being launched not only to 
support delivery of structured and demand driven capacity developments to put in place an 
institutional and robust training delivery system using digital technologies, but also to help in 
enhancing capacity and skills of public servants, through well defined framework of 
competencies and core values. The objective is improved effectiveness of training and 
capacity building programs delivered by central and state level training institutes targeting 
public servants.  
1.4 iGOT 2.0 has resources for online, face to face and blended learning. It will subsume 
the existing iGOT portal hosted on and build upon its existing smart features to further the 
vision of a digital India served by a digital force with significantly more c apabilities. This 
will overcome existing infrastructure bottlenecks, to create an ecosystem where capacity 

3 
 
building efforts reach the last level of officials. The iGOT 2.0 platform will be a digital 
backbone which will allow many other layers and solutions  to be built on top, as the platform 
evolves, paving the way for larger transformations to happen. 
1.5 It is relevant to mention here that in pursuance of the decision of the Empowered 
Group on Augmenting Human Resources and Capacity Building set up by the  Hon’ble Prime 
Minister under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises), DoPT 
has launched a tailored version of iGOT on 07 th April, 2020 to train all the COVID -19 
warriors of India. As on 03 rd June, 2020, 10,52,410 users have been enrolled in iGOT for 
Covid learning platform. 
Further Observation 
1.6 The Committee appreciates the Department for devising more schemes in 
general and Integrated Government Online Training (iGOT) programme in particular 
which aim at augmenting human resou rce potential and improving governance . 
However, it would like to reiterate its recommendation that the Ministry should take 
necessary corrective measures to ensure proportionate and timely disbursement of 
funds.  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The Committ ee does not see any logic for the difference of 12 crore between the 
projection made by UPSC to the Ministry of Finance for the financial year 2020 -21 and 
Budget allocated to them in BE 2020 -21 as UPSC has the distinction of spending more than 
99% of the allocated budgetary amount for the last three financial years. The Committee is of 
the view that full allocation of required funds has to be made in future to UPSC so that the 
most premier recruitment institution of our country is not made to face uncalled for 
hardships due to paucity of funds.                              (para 2.72) 
Action taken 
2.1 Budgetary allocations to the Ministry and its various attached/ subordinate offices are 
made by Ministry of Finance and on the basis of the discussions in the Pre -Budget meeting 
taken by Secretary (Expenditure) with the representatives of the Ministry, Sub ordinate and 
Attached Offices.  
2.2 Observations of the Committee have been noted and in future, M/o Finance would be 
requested to make adequate financial allocations to the UPSC to discharge its obligations 
effectively.    
Further Observation 
2.3 The Comm ittee has noted the reply of the Ministry and hopes that the 
Department would pursue with the Ministry of Finance for providing  additional 
budgetary allocation to UPSC as per their projection at RE stage so that the premier 
recruitment agency can adequately carry out its constitutional mandate. 
 
PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT: 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Committee expresses its concern over significant vacancies in the Indian 
Administrative Service, which is the backbone of the administrative machinery of thi s 

4 
 
country. The Committee is of the view that the induction of IAS officers must keep pace with 
the evolving needs of the Indian administration. Therefore, the Committee strongly 
recommends the Department to bridge the gap between the sanctioned strength an d the in -
position strength and to address the problem of deficit of bureaucrats afflicting the Indian 
administration pronto.                     (Para 3.2)   
Action Taken 
3.1 The occurrence of vacancies in IAS and its filling up is an ongoing process. The 
Government has increased the annual intake of IAS officers to 180 every year through Direct 
Recruitment, since Civil Services Examination (CSE) 2012. Further, vacancies in IAS  under 
Promotion Quota are filled up every year by the Government, based upon a proposal from the 
concerned State Governments and as per the recommendations of the Selection Committee 
Meeting (SCM) convened by Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) for app ointment of 
State Civil Services (SCS) and non -State Civil Services (non -SCS) Officers, by induction 
into IAS.  
Further Observation 
3.2 The Committee is pleased to note that the Government has increased the intake 
of IAS officers to 180 every year since 2012. However, the Committee is of the 
considered view that the increased intake should be commensurate with the whopping 
gap between the sanctioned strength and the in -position strength and it should not be 
fixed at 180 only. The Committee would like the Department to prepare a detailed road 
map elaborating on how long it would take to mitigate the existing gap between the 
sanctioned strength and the in -position strength as per the extant plan and furnish the 
same to it. 
Recommendation/Observation

5.0 The Committee notes that at present, candidates have to appear for multiple 
examinations conducted by multiple agencies at different points of time for similar posts 
resulting in enormous burden on time, effort and cost of youn g people. The Committee is of 
the view that NRA will be the major reform in recruitment to Non -Gazetted posts in 
government jobs and public sector banks. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Government to expedite the process of setting up of NRA and to ensure that the proposal 
materializes soon. Since the examination is broad based and is proposed to be conducted 
online, the Committee recommends that the Department must take necessary measures to 
mitigate the vulnerability of exam infrastructure to malpr actices. The Committee also 
recommends that NRA should be an independent, professional and specialized recruitment 
organisation and that it should be well equipped to discharge its mandate effectively. 
                  (para 3.19)

5.1 Recommendation of the Committee is noted for compliance. 
Further Observation

recommendations of the Committee. The Committee, however, desires to be apprised of

All the state cadres will once again be requested to take timely action for review of the

6.2 Central Civil Services Employees: The Appropriate Authority has the absolute right 
to retire a Governmentservant under FR 56(J), FR 56(I) or Rule 48 (1) (b) of CCS (Pension) 
Rules, 1972 as the case may be, if it is necessary to do so in public interest to strengthen the 
administrative machinery by developing responsible andefficient workers at all levels and 
efficiency, economy and speed in the disposal of Government functions. 
6.3 Government has noted the recommendation of the Committee for undertaking rev iew 
of the performance of the Government servants on regular basis, without any bias and 

8 
 
favouritism. In this regard, instructions have been issued by the Government from time to 
time, requiring the appointing authorities to carry out periodical review of the performance of 
the Central Government servants. All these guidelines/instructions have been placed in public 
domain. Further, these guidelines inter-alia provide that such reviews are to be undertaken in 
each quarter of the year for cases falling due in subsequent six months. The guidelines further 
provide that after carrying out the review, based on the overall personal records of the officer, 
and not confined to Annual Performance Appraisal Report alone, an officer can be 
prematurely retired, on the g rounds of inefficiency and doubtful integrity. Further, 
instructions have also been issued from time to time, inter alia, highlighting the observations 
made by various Courts in the matter. These guidelines provide an enabling framework for 
removal of deadwood, as also to eliminate bias and favouritism while deciding the cases and 
to promote efficiency in the Government.

periodically under FR 56 (j). In CSS cadre, one officer each in the grades of Director, Deputy 
Secretary, Under Secretary and Assistant Section Officer was retired under FR 56 (j) during

6.5 As far as CSSS officers/officials are concerned, so far none has been identified as 
non-performers and of doubtful integrity during past five years and none has been 
prematurely retired on the basis of non -performance and doubtful integrity. CSCS is a

performers or any official with doubtful integrity for premature retirement.

TRAINING INSTITUTIONS: 
Recommendation/Observation 
8.0 The Committee feels that Globalization has brought about paradigmatic 
transformation in government, governance and public administration. Civil Servants are 
expected to deliver under very trying circumstances and with adequate resources. They are 
required to develop new knowledge and skills in order to meet this challenge of globalization. 
Emotional Intelligence can equip and prepare the Civil servants to handle such pressures 

9 
 
and constraints with ease. Thus, the Committee recommends LBSNAA to re-orient its training 
strategy and curriculum aimed at making Civil Servants emotionally intelligent. 
(para 5.2) 
Action Taken

Improvement. Sessions on ‘Emotional Intelligence’ are conducte d, especially for MCTP 
courses. 
8.2 The recommendations of the Committee to LBSNAA to re -orient its training strategy 
and curriculum aimed at making Civil Servants emotionally intelligent, and to recalibrate its 
course content so as to make civil servants ethical and responsible have been noted by the 
Academy / Management faculty for compliance. 
Further Observation 
8.3 The Committee has noted the reply of the Ministry. 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.0 The Committee notes that IIPA is specialized in policy eva luation, service delivery 
and impact analysis studies. The Committee has been apprised that the current practice is to 
submit the findings of research to the Ministry/Department concerned. The Committee is of 
the opinion that a well researched document det ailing how effective a scheme is or how well 
or poorly a scheme is performing, what is working on ground and what is not, should be kept 
in public domain. The Committee believes that providing public access to such research 
findings will enhance transparen cy, increase accountability and strengthen participatory 
governance.                                                       (para 5.14) 
 
Action Taken 
9.1 IIPA undertakes Research Studies/Evaluation of Schemes of various Ministries and 
Departments. The relationship between IIPA and the sponsoring Ministry/Department is 
basically a client relationship. As such, the reports are submitted to the respective 
Ministries/Departments which further take a decision whether putting the Report in public

11.0 The Committee notes that over 48000 cases are still pending disposal and that over

Further Observation 
4.4 The Committee is satisfied with the reply of the Ministry and is in favour of 
roping in subject/domain experts from the private sector as they will bring in more 
expertise into government agencies. However, the Committee is of the considered view 
that the Government should establish a robust mechanism to prevent nepotism and

Recommendation/Observation 
5.0 The Committee notes that 360 degree performance appraisal intends to capture the 
qualities of officers in terms of integrity, capability and general reputation based on an 
appraisal of the Annual Performance Appraisal Report (APAR) by an Expert Committee and 
feedback received from various stakeholders. The Committee notes that such a system of 
empanelment has widened representation in the Central Government to all services. It has 
also eliminated discretion and scope for lobbying associated with senior level positio ns. 
However, the Committee notes that feedback in this process is obtained informally leaving it 
susceptible to manipulations. The Committee observes that the feedback received from 
subordinates and stakeholders may sometimes be biased and can lack objecti vity, 

18 
 
particularly if the officer had an occasion to discipline his subordinate or he was unable to 
meet the unjustified demands of stakeholders. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should take steps to ensure that such biased feedback is not reli ed upon in order 
that honest and deserving civil servants are not victimized.                                    (Para 3.27) 
Action Taken 
5.1 Multi Source Feedback from relevant stakeholders in Empanelment process (360* 
performance appraisal):- The Multi Source Feedback (MSF) system has been introduced with 
an aim at ensuring comprehensive assessment of officers for empanelment to hold senior 
positions in Government. Under it, officers are assessed by an Experts Panel (EP) not only on 
the basis of their ACR/APAR grades but also based on a feedback obtained from a minimum 
of 05 stakeholders including Seniors, Juniors, Peers, External Stakeholders and serving 
Secretaries. MSF is taken on seven clearly defined attributes which include decision making, 
ownership, pro-activeness, delivery, leadership, honesty and suitability for higher positions. 
In case of large variation between feedbacks of stakeholders, the EP may take more feedback 
from additional stakeholders. In addition, overall service record and vigilan ce inputs, etc. 
about the officers are also taken into account. Feedback from a diverse range of stakeholders 
and anonymity and confidentiality in the process ensures objectivity and transparency. 
 
5.2 In order to ensure fairness and objectivity in the process, assessment is done by the EP 
comprising four/five carefully chosen members of very high merit and integrity. The 
feedback obtained by the EP is appended to the final report thus, making it a well -
documented record rather than an informal process.  
5.3 A system of review is in place for officers not empanelled. In such cases, review is 
done by a separate panel of Experts, who obtain fresh MSF from a different set of 
stakeholders. 
5.4 Thus, it may be seen that feedback from diverse range of stakeholders  and anonymity 
and confidentiality in the process under MSF system ensures objectivity, transparency and 
fairness in the empanelment process.

TRAINING INSTITUTIONS: 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.0 The Committee is of the view that civil servants should act in the best interest of the 
public at all times. Though there are laws, Institutions and mechanisms in place to curb 
corruption, it is increasingly being realised that such mechanisms alone are not sufficient to 
instill integrity in them. Thus, the Committee strongly feels that Civil servants should be 
sensitised about ethics and values in pub lic life through training. The Committee 
recommends LBSNAA to recalibrate its course content so as to make civil servants ethical 
and responsible in both interpersonal and intrapersonal realms. The Committee recommends 
LBSNAA that the measures taken to ins till ethics and values in public life in civil servants 
through training may be submitted to the Committee in its Action Taken Note.         
                                                                              (Para 5.3) 
Action Taken 
9.1 The mission of the LBSNAA is ‘To promote good governance by providing quality 
training for building a professional and responsive civil service in a caring, ethical and 
transparent framework’.   In keeping with this mission, it is the constant endeavour of the 
Academy to include the following core values of the Academy in all the inputs in different 
courses being administered here: 
(i)  Serve the Underprivileged : Be humane in your approach while dealing with 
people; be the voice of the underprivileged and be  proactive in addressing any injustice 
against them. You can achieve success in this endeavor if you act with integrity, respect, 
professionalism and collaboration. 
 
(ii) Integrity: Be consistent in your thoughts, words and actions which will make you 
trustworthy. Have courage of conviction and always speak the truth to even the most 
powerful, without fear. Never ever tolerate any degree of corruption, be it in cash, kind or 
intellectual. 
 
(iii) Respect: Embrace diversity of caste, religion, colour, gen der, age, language, region, 
ideology and socio -economic status. Reach out to all with humility and empathy. Be 
emotionally stable, grow with confidence and without arrogance. 
 
(iv) Professionalism: Be judicious and apolitical in your approach; be professio nal and 
completely committed to your job with a bias for action and results; and continuously 
pursue improvement and excellence. 
 
(v)  Collaboration: Collaborate in thoughts and actions by engaging deeply with all to 
evolve consensus. Encourage others, pro mote team spirit and be open to learning from 
others. Take initiative and own responsibility. 
 
9.2 The measures taken to instill ethics and values in public life in civil servants through 
training are as follows: 
1. Exclusive modules / sessions on Ethics, Ethical Dilemmas, Ethics in Public Service 
etc. are organized for the Officer Trainees as a part of the course curriculum.  The 
participants are also expected to write case studies on Ethical Dilemmas in Administration.  

21 
 
These case studies are further util ized as discussion drivers for bringing out the ethical issues 
in governance. 
2. All the Training Courses in the Academy have a heavy component of personal 
awareness and Self Improvement.  Sessions on Ethical Leadership, Emotional Quotient, 
Team Work, Beha vioural Insights for Administrators etc. are conducted.  The purpose of 
these modules / exercises is to delve deeper into the issues of personal ethics and values and 
how they impact governance.  The effort is on Self -awareness i.e. awareness of ones 
behaviour and attitudes, biases etc., which would enable the officer to deliver governance 
which is fair, transparent and humane.  
3. Academy also exposes the young Officer Trainees to eminent Guest Speakers who 
have exhibited very high moral standards in their  public and personal life with the objective 
that the trainees are persuaded to achieve high ethical and moral standards in public 
governance, through “moral suasion”.  
4. In order to cover practical aspects of transparency and fairness in the sphere of pu blic 
governance, and to inculcate a sense of financial integrity and proprietary in the participants, 
modules on Public Procurement, Financial Rules, Conduct Rules, Discipline and Appeal 
Rules etc. are also organized by the Academy.  These form standard in puts in all the courses 
at the Academy.  Through these classes the Officer Trainees acquire the requisite perspective 
and the financial skills needed for ensuring a fair and clean public administration. 
5. Academy believes in imparting training which not o nly makes the officers competent, 
but also imbibes in them an approach to public governance which is humane, sensitive and 
inclusive.  As a part of this endeavour, various modules on Social Inclusion (Gender,

12.0 The Committee notes that Tribunals were established with the objective to provide 
speedy and inexpensive justice to the litigants. However, the level of  pendency in CAT puts 
across a serious point that this basic object of overcoming delays in dispensation of justice is 
far from being achieved. Hence, the Committee recommends the Government to identify the 
root causes of piling up of cases in tribunals an d apprise the Committee of the measures 
taken to cut the backlog of pending cases in the Action Taken note.                        (Para 6.21) 
Action Taken 
12.1 The Central Administrative Tribunal is a quasi -judicial body, created under the 
Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, for the adjudication or trial by Administrative Tribunals 
of disputes and complaints with respect to recruitment and conditions of service o f persons 
appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any 
local or other authority brought under its jurisdiction under section 14(2) of the Act.  
 
12.2 At present, the Tribunal exercises jurisdiction over the Departments of Government of 
India, Union Territories and 214 Boards, Corporation and Societies owned or controlled by 
the Government of India. The Central Administrative Tribunal has 07 regular Benches and 21 
Circuit Benches all over India. 
 
12.3 Since 1985 till December, 2019 about 8,14,796 cases have been instituted and out of 
these, 7,65,831 cases have already been disposed of, which is about 94% of the cases 
instituted during the period. Despite the shortage of Members, 26,040 cases have been 
disposed of against the 24,952 cases instituted during the year 2019, which is about 104.36% 
of the cases instituted during the said period.  
 
12.4 The primary reason of pendency of cases is that decision to be passed by higher courts 
(High Courts and Supreme Court) in similar cases are being awaited by Hon’ble CAT to pass 
decision in large number of similar pending cases. 
 
12.5 Also, another major reason is the vacancies of Members in the Tribunal. As on date, 
there are a total of 27 vacancies of Members (14 -Judicial and 13 -Administrative). For the 
vacancy year 2018, offer of appointment of 06 new Administrative Members have already 
been issued. One of them has assumed the charge of the office. On assumption of charge by 
other 05 Administrative Members, the number of vacancies will come down to 22.  
 
12.6 The process of filling up the vacancies for the year 2019 got deferred due to re -
formulation of the rules made under the Finance Act 2017. The Tribunal, Appellate Tribunal 
and other Authorities (Qualifications, Exper ience and other Conditions of Service of 
Members) Rules, 2020 have recently been notified on 12.02.20 under the Finance Act, 2017 
on implementation of Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated 13.11.19 passed in Civil 
Appeal No.  8588/2019 (Roger Mathew Vs So uth Indian Bank Ltd. & Others). Now, the 
advertisement for inviting applications for the vacancies of Members (CAT) for the vacancy 
year 2019 will be issued shortly.  
 
12.7 It is also to be placed on record that the functioning of the Tribunal is different  than 
those of other regular Courts, where Benches can be constituted by any two Judges. Here in 
the Tribunal, a Division Bench could only be constituted of one Judicial and one 

25 
 
Administrative Member. Thus, the deficiency in either category hampers the fun ctioning of 
the Tribunal. 
 
12.8 The Hon’ble Chairman is closely monitoring the disposal of Benches and also 
impressing upon to make every endeavour to reduce backlog pendency.  
 
12.9 It may be worth mentioning that implementation of Advance Case Informatio n 
System (ACIS) in CAT, which facilitates E -courts facility and includes e -filing, online 
remittance of fee, hearing of the cases through video conferencing at the discretion of the 
Tribunal is currently under progress. Once the ACIS will be operational, M embers of 
different Benches may constitute a Division Bench and hear the cases through video 
conferencing, which may be helpful to reduce the pendency of old cases to some extent.   
Further Observation

Case Information System is operationalized soon.

ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES: 
Recommendation/Observation 
12.0 The Right of Citizens for Time -bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal 
of their Grievances Bill, 2011 is essentially citizen centric and will ensure time bound 
delivery of Goods and services as well as facilitate timely redressal of grievan ces besides 
strengthening accountability and promoting transparency. The Committee in its 95th Report 
recommended the Government to consider the reintroduction of the said Bill and till then 
implement the proposed scheme without any further delay. The Comm ittee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation.                    (Para 7.12) 
Action Taken 
12.1 A CoS note on Delivery of Services and Grievances Redressal Scheme was referred 
to the Cabinet Secretariat. The proposal is being examined in consultation with the concerned 
authorities for appropriate action.  However, DARPG has taken the following measures to 
improve effectiveness of service delivery and grievance redressal: 
Service Delivery:  DARPG in its efforts to provide more responsive and citizen -
friendly governance coordinates with the Central Ministries to formulate and 
operationalise Citizen’s Charters.   Recently the Ministry has undertaken certain 
steps on Citizen Charter of Ministry of External Affairs and Central Board of 
Direct Taxes to review their Citizen’s Charters.  Based on this, the charter of both 
the organizations have been revamped to make them one stop information 
platform. DARPG is regularly  taking meetings with   Ministries on review and 
updation of their Citizen’s Charter. 
Public Grievances: DARPG has initiated the CPGRAMS Reforms by process re -
engineering of existing CPGRAMS for faster and qualitative resolution of 
grievances. The CPGRAMS 7.0 facilitate direct mapping of grievances with  last 
mile  officer  responsible for resolution to r educe the   disposal time , enable 
automatic escalation of the grievance to the next higher level if not resolved by the 
sub-ordinate office within the stipulated timeframe and  enable better identification 
of gaps between policy and delivery. 
12.2 The reform has already been implemented in 9 Ministries / Departments - Department 
of Posts, Telecom, DFS (Banking & Insurance), M/ Road Transport and Highways, M/ 
External Affairs, D/ School Education and literacy, M/ Health & FW and M/ Petroleum.   
Dept. of Posts reported that CPGRAM reforms have covered 1.5 lac post offices, saving 2323 
Mondays and reduced timelines of disposal substantially. 

40 
 
12.3 The reform would be implemented in all other Ministry/Departments/Organizations in 
phased manner. 
12.4 Further NIC has  developed web APIs to facilitate integration of State Grievance 
Portals with CPGRAMS. 8 States portals have been integrated so far.  
Further Observation  
12.5 The Committee is appreciative of the initiatives taken by DARPG to improve 
service delivery and facilitate speedy redressal of grievances. However, the Committee 
observes that the Ministry has avoided giving any reply in respect of the 
recommendation made by the Committee for reintroduction of the Right of Citizens for 
Time-bound Delivery of Goods an d Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 
2011. The Committee reiterates its recommendation as it believes that passage and 
enactment of this bill will ensure time bound delivery of Goods and services and 
facilitate timely redressal of grievances for citizens and strengthen accountability and 
promote transparency. The Committee would like to be apprised of the view of the 
Ministry in this regard.

The Committee recommends that the ISTM should be adequately staffed and fund 
should not be a constraint in this regard. The Committee hopes that all the vacant 
positions will be filled up during this financial year.                           (Para 6.4) 
 
39. The Committee recommends that adequate funds should be provided to IIPA so 
that it can discharge its mandate effectively. The Committee recommends the 
Department to pursue with the Ministry of Fi nance to allocate additional funds to 
IIPA as per its projected demand at RE stage as any shortfall in allocation will 
adversely affect IIPA’s capacity to invest in training and research.   (Para 7.2) 
 
40. The Committee has noted that Rs 781.01 Cr was allocated to CBI in BE 2019 -20, a 
marginal increase from Rs 778.93 Cr allocated in 2018 -19. Again, only Rs. 802.79 
Cr have been allocated to CBI against the projected demand of Rs. 1386.26 Cr. 
The Committee und erstands that the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), a 
premium investigating arm of the Government investigates large number of 
sensitive, high -profile corruption and economic fraud cases against public 
servants, private persons, firms. Besides this, C BI also probes and pursues several 

46 
 
extradition cases against fugitive economic offenders as well as criminals in courts 
of other countries. Such investigation and probes require large scale deployment of 
human resources and funds. The Committee hopes that additional funds will be 
provided to the premier investigation agency at RE stage so that it can discharge 
its tremendous responsibilities without any hindrance.                (Para 8.2) 
 
41. The Committee has noted the reply of the Ministry. The Committee in  its previous 
Reports including its 95 th Report on Demands for Grants (2018 -19) had expressed 
its displeasure over slow pace of utilisation of funds by CBI. The Committee noted 
that  on account of underutilisation or slow pace of utilization of funds , allocations 
to CBI were reduced at the RE stage and consequently the Budget Estimates of 
next year are also reduced and it happened this financial year also. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that a robust monitoring mechanism 
should be set up in the organisation to monitor the pace of implementation of 
schemes and projects from start to finish and consequently proper utilisation of 
funds is ensured.           (Para 9.2) 
 
42. The Committee is not satisfied with the plain reply of the Ministry. The Committee 
is of the view that The Centralised Technology Vertical (CTV) project, which aims 
to facilitate real-time information sharing with investigators across the country, is 
an important project of CBI and it should be operationalized at the earliest. 
Besides this,  International Centre of Excellence in Forensic Science and 
International Centre of Excellence in Investigation should also be established soon. 
The Committee should be apprised of the steps taken for completion of both the 
projects and hurdles being faced by the Ministry in this regard.              (Para 10.2) 
 
43. The Committee takes note of the reply of the Ministry delineating the progress 
made with regard to addressing the problems of infrastructure and human 
resource deficits nagging CAT Infrast ructure Deficit. The Committee also takes 
note of the fact that out of seventeen benches, only eight benches are functioning 
from their own buildings, four benches are functioning from Government 
buildings and rest five Benches are functioning from rented buildings. The 
Committee is of the considered view that all nine benches including those which 
are functioning from Government buildings on rent or otherwise should have their 
own buildings and all necessary steps such as identification of sites, construct ion of 
buildings etc should be completed in time bound manner, however, priority should 
be given to benches which are functioning from rented buildings.           (Para 11.6) 
 
44. The Committee further notes that out of 66 sanctioned posts of Hon’ble Chairman/ 
Members (33 -Judicial and 33 -Administrative) 27 posts (14 -Judicial & 13 -
Administrative) of Hon’ble Members are vacant in various Benches and more 
vacancies are likely to arise this year. The Committee strongly recommends that 
all the vacancies should be fi lled up on priority basis at the earliest to reduce 
arrears and backlogs of cases.                                                  (Para 11.7) 
 
45. The Committee is appreciative of the initiatives taken by DARPG to improve 
service delivery and facilitate speedy redressal of grievances. However, the 
Committee observes that the Ministry has avoided giving any reply in respect of 
the recommendation made by the Committee for reintroduction of the Right of 
Citizens for Time -bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their 

47 
 
Grievances Bill, 2011. The Committee reiterates its recommendation as it believes 
that passage and enactment of this bill will  ensure time bound delivery of Goods 
and services and facilitate timely redressal of grievances for citizens and 
strengthen accountability and promote transparency. The Committee would like 
to be apprised of the view of the Ministry in this regard.                         (Para 12.5)
