3.39 The Committee notes that based on an independent third party comprehensive 
review of the root cause of the pensioners' grievances the DPPW has initiated key 
reforms like complete digitalization of pension process and improvement in submission 
of Life Certificate by pensioners. The Committee appreciates such initiatives being 
taken up by the Department based on their learning from pensioners' grievances. 
3.40 The Committee observes that as per last five years data provided by the 
Department on satisfaction ratings, about 40% of complainants have rated their 
grievance redressal as poor. Such ratings reflect poorly on the overall grievance 
handling by different organizations. Further, about twelve Ministries/Departments in 
the year 2021 and twenty two Ministries/Departments in the year 2020 have failed to 
resolve more than 30% of pensioners' grievances pertaining to them within the 
stipulated time. This shows apathy of those organizations towards handling of 
pensioners' grievances and the Committee feels dismayed over indifference shown by 
government officials to the grievances of their retired colleagues.  
3.41 The Committee accordingly recommends the DPPW to develop a 
mechanism/guidelines/policy to ensure accountability of the government officials 
dealing with the pensioners' grievances and suggest action against the erring officials. 
The appellate authority should be empowered to award monetary penalties and 
sanction disciplinary action against those officials who are habitually responsible for 
delayed action or summary disposal of grievances without any qualitative action.  
II. PENSION ADALATS 
3.42 This Department had started the unique experiment of holding Pension Adalats to 
resolve chronic grievances of Central Govt. Pensioners, falling within the four walls of extant 
policy. These Adalats, as the term might sound, do not have any judicial or quasi-judicial 
powers but have proved a highly successful mode of grievance resolution. All the stake-
holders of a particular grievance are invited on a single table viz. the concerned 

 37 
Ministry/Department, the Pay & Accounts Officer of the concerned Department, the CPAO 
(Central Pension Accounts Officer, Ministry of Finance), the concerned Bank and the 
Pensioner or his/her representative and they resolve the case across the table. 
3.43 The Departmental Parliamentary Standing Committee for Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances & Pensions in its 95th Report appreciated the system of holding Pension 
Adalats and suggested that a day may be dedicated to the Pensioners, as part of good 
governance, and efforts be made to minimize their grievances. The Committee suggested 
holding Pension Adalats, on a particular day, across Ministries, throughout the country, with 
this objective in view.

3.45 As per the data provided by the Department on disposal of pension grievances 
during Pension Adalats, their resolution rates are significantly high. This perhaps is due 
to the fact that all stakeholders of a particular grievance are invited on a single table, 
the grievances are resolved quickly. Considering this performance, as recommended by 
the Committee in its 106th report, the Committee once again reiterates that such Pension 
Adalats should be held more regularly and frequently. Further, the experience gained 
during COVID times, the practice of holding Pension Adalats through video 
conferencing should be promoted.  
III. SANKALP 
3.46 A number of pensioners feel the loss of a daily routine as well as of a feeling of not 
being wanted.  Keeping these factors in mind a new initiative of the Department, christened 
as Sankalp, has been taken up to prepare them for post-retirement life and channelize 

 38 
experiences and skill of retired Government servants towards meaningful interventions in 
Society.  
3.47 Under this initiative the Department is also conducting Pre-Retirement Counseling 
Sessions (PRCs) for employees retiring in near future. 47 PRCs have been conducted till date 
which benefited 5972 retiring/retired personnel of various Ministries and Departments of 
Government of India. PRC covers aspects relating to timely payment of pension and 
processing formalities, CGHS benefits available to pensioners, investment options, income 
tax incentives for senior citizens/pensioners, preparation of Will and post retirement 
voluntary effort. 
IV. ANUBHAV  
3.48 Anubhav is a platform for retiring government employees to share their experience of 
working with the Government.  It is envisaged that Anubhav will be nurtured as a tool for 
creating institutional memory. Till date 92 organizations have registered, 7320 write-ups have 
been published and 5401 write-ups which have been uploaded and are waiting to be 
published.  
3.49 An Annual Award Scheme to incentivize and encourage more retiring employees to 
submit their write-ups was introduced. Till date 4 award ceremonies have been organized in 
which 35 awardees was conferred appreciation for their Anubhav write-ups. 
V. PENSIONERS’ ASSOCIATIONS 
3.50 While initiating the Pensioners‟ Portal, it was envisaged to engage a large number of 
Pensioners‟ Associations in the successful implementation and continuing operation of the 
above mechanism, so as to make it largely self-sustaining. DoPPW has identified 46 
Pensioners‟ Associations from across the country and involved them for effective 
implementation of the Pensioners Portal.  These Associations help pensioners in filing their 
grievances online through CPENGRAMS, pursue the cases with the concerned authorities at 
various levels and also take up various activities for the welfare of pensioners besides 
increasing general awareness amongst retiring and retired Govt. servants about retirement and 
pension related matters.  
3.51 The Committee commends the overall performance of the Department of 
Pension and Pensioners Welfare and hopes that it will continue with its good work to 
bring about 'ease of living' for pensioners, especially for super senior citizens and family 
pensioners.

CHAPTER - III - POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS & PUBLIC GRIEVANCES 
(DARPG) 
 
Public Grievances 
 
Centralized Public Grievances Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS)  
5. The Committee is of the view that no government can claim itself to be 
accountable, responsive and user-friendly unless it has established an efficient and 
effective grievance redress mechanism. In fact, the efficiency and effectiveness of any 
organization can be measured by its grievance redressal mechanism as it provides 
important feedback on its working. Thus grievance redressal should be one of the core 
components of good governance.  
(Para 3.4) 
6. The Committee also observes that CPGRAMS has become the mainstay of 
public grievance edifice of the country. The Committee notes that over the years the 
Department has made many significant improvements in the grievance redressal 
system. Citizens are now being able to benefit from the portal by getting their 
grievances redressed in a time-bound manner. The Department has brought to the 
notice of the Committee several instances where citizens have got redressal of their 
grievances promptly and timely through the portal during the lockdowns due to 
pandemic.  
(Para 3.5) 

 41 
7. The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has implemented most of 
its recommendations like reduction in redressal period from 60 to 45 days, introduction 
of appellate mechanism, integration of the portal with the portals of states and thus 
achieving one nation - one portal goal, making available the CPGRAMS website in 
regional languages, initiating preparation of a 'Grievance Redressal Index', creating a 
facility for filing grievance via speech to text method etc. The Committee therefore 
appreciates and lauds the efforts of the Department for continuously improving and 
bringing about thoughtful changes in the grievance redressal system.  
(Para 3.6) 
8. However, it has come to the notice of the Committee that a large part of 
grievances are being disposed off in a routine and ad-hoc manner and the complainant 
remains dissatisfied with the redressal. The Committee feels that the Public Grievances 
should be resolved in a professional and satisfactory manner. There is a need to fix 
accountability on the decision making authorities. In the event of unsatisfactory 
redressal of the grievances, the public usually tend to approach courts for redressal of 
their grievances which increases the burden of courts, so the Committee desires every 
endeavour should be made to resolve grievances to the satisfaction of the complainant. 
Accordingly, the Committee recommends the department to develop mechanism to 
ensure accountability of the government officials dealing with the citizen's grievances. 
(Para 3.7) 
9. The Committee also takes note of the fact that a very large number of the public 
grievances are limited to some specific aspects of certain organizations/Departments. 
The Committee desires that all those areas where a large number of grievances are 
received,  should be examined and in those common areas of grievances, after analyzing 
the root cause, systemic changes wherever necessary should be brought without any 
delay which in turn will reduce the volume of grievances to a large extent.  
(Para 3.8) 
10. More and more people are becoming aware of the CPGRAMS, which may be 
gauged from the ever increasing number of grievances received every year on the 
portal. However, a large number of citizens are still not aware of the CPGRAMS; 
especially in the rural and semi-urban areas the awareness about it is very low or 
negligible. The Committee therefore recommends that every effort should be made to 
advertise on a large scale in mass media including newspapers, FM radio, social media 
etc. about CPGRAMS in the scheduled languages. 
(Para 3.9) 
11. Lastly, on the recommendations of this Committee, the Department has recently 
made available the CPGRAMS portal in three regional languages i.e.  Bengali, Gujarati 
and Marathi. The Committee recommends that the Department should make available 
the portal in other regional languages on priority basis.  
(Para 3.10) 

 42 
Time Bound Delivery of Services 
12. The Committee, therefore, recommends the government to bring a scheme for a 
time-bound delivery of goods and services for citizens. Initially the scheme may be 
started by including a few basic services only, which may later be expanded to include 
other services also. The Scheme should include appropriate measures for reward and 
punishment of government functionaries so that it remains effective.  
(Para 3.12) 
E-Office - Mission Mode Project 
13. The Committee observes that e-Office is one of the key e-Governance reforms 
brought by the Department in the recent past. It has helped not only in making the 
government's work more faster and more efficient, but has also made a marked 
difference in the decision making process. It has proven its worth during the recent 
lockdowns due to COVID pandemic in the work-from-home scenario. 
(Para 3.16) 
14. The Committee is therefore of the view that the e-office should be implemented 
in all Central Government Ministries / Departments / organizations on priority basis. 
Proper training on e-Office should be imparted to the officials.  Every effort must be 
made to encourage officials to carry out their office work through e-office only. Further, 
at an appropriate time, it should be made binding for all Government 
Departments/organizations, in a phased manner, to carry out all their official work 
through e-office only.  
(Para 3.17) 
15. The Department, along with NIC/MeitY should also keep on improving the e-
office software based on the inputs received from all stakeholders, on a continuous 
basis. The e-office should also be made compatible with all widely used browsers. As e-
office has the potential for making lot of savings for the government in terms of office 
space, stationery etc., the Committee therefore, recommends the DARPG to approach 
the MoF, with proper justifications, and seek funds to implement the e-office project on 
a faster pace in all Ministries.  
(Para 3.18) 
Administrative Reforms 
16. The Committee observes that apathy of civil servants in implementation of 
Government schemes/programmes is one of the major impediments in the 
implementation of government schemes and delivery of services and therefore , 
recommends DARPG to make appropriate programmes and initiatives for instilling 
right public service delivery attitude in civil servants by strengthening their behavioural 
competency.

CHAPTER - I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by 
the British Parliament and it is one of the oldest limbs of the Government of India. In 
accordance with the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry 
comprises three Departments under the overall charge of the Law and Justice Minister 
assisted by a Minister of State. Each department is administratively headed by an independent 
Secretary. 
 
1.1.  The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in administration 
of justice; giving legal advice to Government of India and defend Government of India in 
various Courts and Tribunals and draft Supreme and Subordinate form of legislations for 
Government of India, etc. 
1.2. In this report, the demands allocated to Legislative Department (Demand No. 65) and 
Election Commission of India (Demand No. 66) has been analyzed and recommendations of 
the Committee have been made at the end of each heading/sub-headings. 
1.3. Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative 
business of the Union Government is concerned. It ensures smooth and speedy processing of 
legislative proposals of various administrative Departments and Ministries.  
 
1.4. This Department not only performs functions as a servicing Department for drafting 
Bills on behalf of Ministries and Departments of the Government of India, but also initiates 
legislative proposals in respect of the matters with which it is administrati vely concerned. 
This Department also drafts the Finance Bill to give effect to the financial proposals of the 
Central Government every year, which is undertaken in the Legislative Department on the 
budget proposals being brought before it by the Ministry o f Finance. For the purposes of

convenience, the various subjects on which Bills are drafted in the Legislative Department at 
the behest of administrative Ministries/ Departments are broadly categorised as under:-  
(a) Constitutional amendments;  
(b) Economic and corporate laws;  
(c) Civil Procedure and other social welfare legislation;  
(d) Repeal of obsolete laws; and  
(e) Miscellaneous laws. 
 
1.5. Further, Ordinance promulgated by the President of India, Regulation made by 
President of India for Union Territories, Electoral Laws and Electoral reforms, maintenance 
of the updated Central Legislation under Bharat Sanhita (India Code) and authoritative 
translation of Central Legislations and Constitution of India in languages specified in the 
Eight Schedule to the Constitution under the Authoritative Text (Central Laws) Act 1973, 
publication and preparation of standard legal terminology, delimitation of Parliamentary and 
Legislative Assembly Constituencies, etc. are also assigned to the Department under 
Allocation of Business Rules, 1961. The Department also imparts training in legislative 
drafting to Officers of the Union/State Government and UT administration through the 
Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR). 
 
1.6. It inter-alia administers Personal laws, Electoral laws, the Indian Contract Act, 1872, 
the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the Evidence Act, 1872, the Indian Trust Act, 1882, the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Limitation Act, 1963, the Election Commission (Conditions of 
Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991, the 
Representation of People Act, 1950 and the Representation of People Act, 1951. It also 
facilitates procurement of Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) for the Election Commission of 
India, Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) Machines and reimbursement of election 
expenditure to State Governments and UT administrations. 
1.7. Legislative Department does not have any statutory or autonomous body under its 
control. It has two other wings under it, namely, the Official Languages Wing and Vidhi 
Sahitya Prakashan, which are responsible  for the progressive use of Hindi and other 
Scheduled languages:- 
(i) Official Languages Wing (OLW): The Official Languages Wing has been entrusted 
with the preparation and publication of standard legal terminologies and for translating into 
Hindi language of Central Acts and Ordinances and Subordinate legislations, etc. under the 

 
10 
Official Languages Act, 1963. This Wing is also responsible for translation of the Central 
Acts, ordinances, etc., into the Official Languages as specified in the 8th Schedule to the 
Constitution. 
(ii) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP): The Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan is mainly concerned 
with bringing out authoritative Hindi version of select reportable judgements of the Supreme 
Court and the High Courts, with the objective of promoting the progressive use of Hindi in 
the legal field. It brings out various publications of legal literature in Hindi and also holds 
exhibitions for giving wide publicity to legal literatures available in Hindi and to promote 
their sales. 
1.8. The organisational set -up of the Legislative Department includes the Secretary, 
Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary &  Legislative Counsel, Additional Legislative Counsel, 
Deputy Legislative Counsel and Assistant Legislative Counsel and other supporting staff. The 
work relating to legislative drafting, scrutiny and vetting of subordinate legislation have been 
distributed among various Legislative Groups, and each group is headed by a Joint Secretary 
& Legislative Counsel or Additional Secretary. The Secretary of the Legislative Department 
also acts as the Chief Parliamentary Counsel and the Additional Secretary is in -charge of all 
subordinate legislation. 
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
1.9. The Legislative Department is the administrative Department for the Election 
Commission of India, an autonomous constitutional authority created under Article 324 of 
Constitution for superintendence, direction, control of elections to Parliament, State 
legislatures, and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President of India.  
1.10. The Election Commission of India is a multimember body (since 1993) headed by the 
Chief Election Commissioner, who acts as Chairman of the Commission. The Chief Election 
Commissioner and Election Commissioners are appointed by the President of India and have 
tenure of six years, or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The Commission is 
assisted by Deputy Election Commissioners, Chief Electoral Officers (CEO), District 
Election Officers (DEO) and Electoral Registration Officers (ERO), appointed by the 
Election Commission under Representation of People Act, 1951.  
1.11. It registers political parties and allots symbols to them and ensures inner party 
democracy in their functioning by insisting organizational elections at periodic intervals. 
Political parties registered with the Commission are granted recognition at the State and 

 
11 
National levels on the basis of their poll performance at general elections according to criteria 
specified by it. It implements Model Code of Conduct (MCC) for smooth conduct of free and 
fair elections. It also observes 25th January as National Voters' Day to encourage young 
electors to take part in election process.  
1.12. The electoral expenses on account of conduct of elections to the House of the People 
and the State Legislative Assembly are borne by the Central Government and the concerned 
State Government, and case of simultaneous elections, the expenditure is to be sha red on 
50:50 basis between Central and the concerned State Government. The initial expenditure is 
borne by the respective State Governments, and on submission of the audited report, the 
Central Government’s share is reimbursed through the Legislative Department.  
1.13. The Election Commission has its independent Secretariat for the work relating to the 
smooth conduct of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, and t here is an exclusive 
demand (Demand No. 66) under which budgetary allocation is sought for running the 
activities of Election Commission of India.

Legislative Impact Assessment 
3.13. Legislative Impact Assessment involves making a comprehensive and systematic 
analysis of the actual impact of the legislation relative to the objects identified at the time of 
its passage. Legislative Impact Assessment broadly covers two stages, namely, ex ante 
assessment and ex post assessment. Ex ante assessment involves making an assessment of the 
anticipated outcomes of the proposed legislation while ex post assessment, also known as 
Post Legislative Scrutiny is the assessment of the actual impact of th e legislation relative to

assessment may be continuous. The objective of the entire LIA exercise is to determine

3.14. The Department in its written replies to the Committee has submitted that it is merely 
a service provider department catering its drafting services to the Ministries/Departme nts of 
the Government of India and pre -legislative consultations, legislative impact analysis or post 
legislative consultation are within the domain of the concerned Ministries/Departments, and 
therefore, Legislative Impact Assessment would have to be done  by that concerned 
Ministry/Department which initiates the legislation. 
 
3.15. The Committee observes that this Department is involved in examining new 
legislations for different Ministries/Departments and also for repealing of obsolete laws. 
The Committee  in its 101 st Report on Demands for Grants (2020 -21) had made 
observations with regard to drafting errors and ambiguity in law/statutes and desired 
for pre-legislative consultation and periodic review of legislations.  The Committee is of 
the view that legislation enacted are not able to keep pace with changing socio -economic 
developments leading to excessive litigations, financial loss to exchequer, disconnect 
with social milieu and so forth.  
 
3.16. The Committee desires that a general consensus is requir ed on the issue of 
Legislative Impact Assessment (LIA), and accordingly of the considered view that there 
has to be a nodal Ministry/Department for dealing with the issues related to LIA, and 
believes that the Legislative Department, due to its expertise i n legislative/cabinet note 
drafting is the most suitable Department under the Government of India for the 
purpose. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to prepare a white 
paper on the Legislative Impact Assessment in the country by taking learning 
experiences of other developed countries.

3.25. As per the  Article 324(1) of the Constitution of India, the electoral rolls for 
Parliament and State Legislatures is prepared by the Election Commission of India,  whereas 
Articles 243K and 243ZA empowers State Election Commissions (SECs) to prepare electoral 
rolls for panchayats/local urban body elections.

electoral roll, though in different forms i.e., Maharashtra and Goa use the same roll, while 
others publish draft and receive claims and objections and then prepare their own final roll. 
The ECI has also been facilitating the SECs by sharing electoral database with them, as and 
when they make a request to the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) of the concerned state. 
3.27. The Election Commission of India (ECI) in its communication to the Government in the 
year 1999 and again in 2004 made reference for creation of Common Electoral Roll. The Law 
Commission of India in its 255 th Report on Electoral Reforms’ (2015) also endorsed the idea 
of Common Electoral Roll. This Committee in its earlier reports, including  the recent 107 th 
and 109th, had also dealt with the issue of Common Electoral Roll. 
3.28. There is a Common Electoral Roll for both Lok Sabha and State Legislative 
Assembly elections as per the Section 13D of the Representation of People Act, 1950, 
according to which the electoral roll for every parliamentary constituency shall consist of the 
electoral rolls for all the Assembly constituencies within it and it shall not be necessary to 
separately prepare or revise the electoral roll for any such parliamentary constituency.  
3.29. The Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 amended the Representation of the 
People Act, 1950 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Section 14(b) of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1950 has been amended and now four qu alifying dates- the 
1st day of January, the 1st day of April, the 1st day of July and the 1st day of October have 
been inserted for preparation and revision of electoral roll. Under Section 23 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951, new sub -clauses (4), (5) & (6) have been added for 
linking/authenticating Aadhar with the electoral roll. 
3.30. The Committee notes that around majority of States/UTs are already using the 
Electoral Roll prepared by Election Commission of India for conducting elections to  their 
Local Bodies elections which are conducted by the State Election Commissions.  
 

 
28 
3.31. The Committee in its previous reports had recommended the Department/ECI 
for a Common Electoral Roll from Parliamentary to local body elections, and 
accordingly, a ppreciates the Department/ECI for sensitizing the Government in 
bringing the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 to provide multiple qualifying dates 
for preparation and revision of electoral roll, thereby, encouraging the States to adopt 
the Common Electo ral Rolls. The Committee is of the view that since the relevant 
statutes have already been amended, the Department/ECI may pursue with the 
remaining State Governments/UTs to implement the common electoral roll. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
29 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
 
Overview of the Budgetary Allocations 
 1.     The Committee observes that allocation to the Official Language Wing (OLW) has 
marginally increased from the Financial Year (2020 -21) to (2021 -22), except in the 
forthcoming financial year (2022 -23), which has seen increase of 25.36 percent over the  
current financial year. Whereas for the Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP), the allocation 
has remained constant in the current and preceding financial year, except allocation of 
Rs. 1.00 crore (14.28 percent) increased in the forthcoming financial year. These  wings 
of the Department play a very important and significant role in translation of Central 
Acts, Ordinances and Subordinate legislation in Hindi and other Eight Scheduled 
languages, and also in translation of judgements of Supreme Court and High Courts in 
Hindi.                                                                                                                           (Para 2.7) 
 
2.  In view of the above, the Committee feels that the static allocations made to these 
Wings over the years may  be due to their under -performance and non -initiation of any 
major new initiatives. The Committee therefore feels that these wings needs to be 
strengthened and, accordingly, recommends the Department to take appropriate steps, 
so that new initiatives can b e initiated by these Wings and the allocation made can be 
optimally utilised.                                                                                                      (Para 2.8) 
3. The Committee observes wide fluctuations in allocation under t he various heads 
of election expenses over the years in BE & RE. It is also observed that allocations for 
‘Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs)’ and ‘EVMs Professional Services’ has been 
drastically reduced in BE (2022 -23) over the projections made to th e Ministry of 
Finance. Further, the Committee is not satisfied with the rationale furnished by the 
Department/ECI that the allocations under the Revenue head in BE (2022 -23) for 
electoral expenses will not adversely affect the work of the Department as aud it 
certificates takes around 2 -3 years. If this was the rationale, then the Committee 
couldn’t fathom as to why projection of Rs 1594.60 crore for ‘Elections 
(Reimbursement to State/UTs) was made to the Ministry of Finance initially.   
                                                                                       (Para 2.11) 
4. The Committee feels that reductions in allocations under the head may be due to 

 
30 
inaccurate projection or inflation of funds required and thereby, failure of the 
Department/ECI to justify its projection to the Ministry of Finance. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that while making projections to the Ministry of Finance in 
future, the Department should ensure that its projection are rational and appropriate to 
meet its requirements.                              (Para 2.12) 
5. The Committee observes that as against an allocation of Rs. 253.00 crore in the 
current Financial Year, the expenditure of the ECI till 31st January, 2022 is only Rs. 
158.74 crore (63 percent approx.). The Committee observes that out of the total 
allocation of Rs. 7.00 crore for capital expenditure in the current financial year; the ECI 
has not been able to spend a single rupee till 31st January, 2022. The Committee 
understands that expenditure under the capital head is directly linked with the external 
agencies like CPWD and NBCC for construction of building for ECI at Dwarka, 
however, the Committee  fails to understand why only Rs. 158.74 has been spent under 
the Revenue head which is well within the control of ECI, and accordingly, the 
Committee recommends ECI to furnish cogent reasons for under-utilisation of funds 
allocated to it under the Revenue head.        
                                                                                                             (Para 2.17) 
6. The Committee also observes allocations have been reduced under Revenue 
heads- Information Technology, Voters’ Awareness, and Training of ECI, which the 
Committee believes are important components of electoral processes. The Committee 
feels that reduction in allocations under the Revenue Expenditure for the forthcoming 
financial year vis-à-vis projection to the Ministry of Finance may be due to the inability 
of the ECI to spend the allocations made for various heads in the current financial year. 
                     (Para 2.18) 
7. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the ECI to improve its spending 
capacity on various activities, as non- expenditure of amount allocated reflects under-
performance of activities/under-utilisation of resources. The Committee is therefore of 
the view that an important institution like ECI should not be forced to limit its activities 
due to financial constraints and recommends the Department/ECI to approach the 
Ministry of Finance for enhanced allocation during the RE stage, especially for 
Information Technology and Voters’ Awareness and Training.                        (Para 2.19) 
Staff Strength in the Department 

 
31 
8. The Committee observes that posts in the Department are vacant due to various 
reasons, and feels that the Department needs to wholeheartedly pursue the issue with 
various authorities engaged in recruitin g and posting of staff to fill -up the vacant 
positions. Further, the Committee feels that recruitment process may be initiated in 
advance in anticipation of likely retirement/vacancy positions to avoid delays and, 
recommends that the Department should forw ard details of vacancy/anticipated 
vacancy positions in advance to the recruiting/cadre controlling authorities.  
(Para 3.4) 
Translation of Constitution of India/Statutes in Scheduled Languages 
9. The Committee in its previous reports, including 101st and 107th, on Demands for 
Grants had expressed its anguish over the lukewarm approach of the Department with 
regard to translation of Constitution and Central Government Acts in Scheduled 
Languages. The Committee observes that no noticeable improvement in the translation 
work has been made in Scheduled Languages or updation work of Constitution of India 
in some Scheduled Languages, like Odia and Sanskrit language. The Committee wishes 
to point out that it was last undertaken around 35 -40 years ago. In this way,  the 
Department is not doing justice to these Scheduled languages. The Committee feels 
priority should be accorded for translating/updating Constitution of India and other 
Central Acts in Odia and Sanskrit at the earliest.                          (Para 3.10) 
10. The Committee also doesn’t agree with the rationale of the Department that the 
process of translation is slow due to ongoing Covid -19 pandemic situation as it observes 
that as on date, the Constitution of India has been translated only in 16 Schedu led 
Languages and further translation/updation work in scheduled language are pending 
for decades. The Committee feels that, instead of blaming the Covid -19 pandemic, 
which is a recent phenomenon, the Legislative Department needs to improve its 
organisational efficiency and get the Constitution of India translated/updated in all the 
regional languages without further delay.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends 
the Department to fix a timeframe for completing the translation/updation of 
Constitution of In dia in all the scheduled languages and apprise this Committee in this 
regard while furnishing the Action Taken Replies.                          (Para 3.11) 
11. The Committee also observes that posts of language officer are vacant for 
Assamese, Gujarati, K anada, Odia, Urdu, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Konkani, Nepali and 
Manipuri. Further, no post of language officers have been sanctioned for Bodo, 

 
32 
Santhali, Maithali, Dogri and Kashmiri languages. The Committee is surprised to note 
that no post/s for language officer s has been created in the Department for Kashmiri 
language (1950), which was included in the Eighth Schedule more than 70 years ago. 
Further, even after 17 years of inclusion in the Eight Schedule, no posts of languages 
officers have been created for Bodo, Santhali, Maithali,  and Dogri, despite having large 
number of people speaking these Scheduled Languages viz. Maithali ( 12,179,122), 
Santhali (6,469,600), Kashmiri (5,527,698), Dogri (2,282,589), and Bodo  (1,350,478)3. 
The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department not only to fill -up the vacant 
position of language officers in the Department  and also approach appropriate 
authorities for creating posts of language officers for Bodo, Santhali, Maithali, Dogri 
and Kasmiri languages without any further delay.                                    (Para 3.12) 
Legislative Impact Assessment 
12. The Committee observes that this Department is involved in examining new 
legislations for different Ministries/Departments and als o for repealing of obsolete laws.

observations with regard to drafting errors and ambiguity in law/statutes and desired 
for pre-legislative consultation and periodic review of legis lations.  The Committee is of 
the view that legislation enacted are not able to keep pace with changing socio -economic 
developments leading to excessive litigations, financial loss to exchequer, disconnect 
with social milieu and so forth.                                                                               (Para 3.15)

Legislative Impact Assessment (LIA), and accordingly of the considered view that there 
has to be a noda l Ministry/Department for dealing with the issues related to LIA, and 
believes that the Legislative Department, due to its expertise in legislative/cabinet note 
drafting is the most suitable Department under the Government of India for the 
purpose. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to prepare a white 
paper on the Legislative Impact Assessment in the country by taking learning 
experiences of other developed countries.                                                             (Para 3.16)

CHAPTER - I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by 
the British Parliament and it is one of the oldest limbs of the Government of India. In 
accordance with the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry 
comprises the following three Departments under the overall charge of the Law and Justice 
Minister assisted by a Minister of State. Each of the three departments is administratively 
headed by an independent Secretary. 
 
 
 
1.1. The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in administration 
of justice; furnishing legal advice to Government of India and defend Government of India in 
various Courts and Tribunals and draft Supreme and Subordinate form of legislations for 
Government of India, etc. 
1.2. In this report, the demands allocated to Department of Legal Affairs (Demand No. 65) 
have been analyzed and recommendations of the Committee have been made at the end of 
each heading/sub-headings. 
1.3. The Department of Legal Affairs has a two-tier set-up, namely, the Main Secretariat at 
New Delhi and Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru. The nature 
of duties discharged by the Department is broadly classified into two areas - Advice work and 
Litigation work.  The Main Secretariat is headed by the Law Secretary, followed by 
Additional Secretaries, Joint Secretary and Legal Advisers and other Legal Advisers at 
various levels.  
1.4. The Department tenders legal advice to all Ministries and Departments of the 
Government of India. The legal advice team of the Department is generally headed by an 
Additional Secretary or a Joint Secretary & Legal Adviser, who, in turn, is assisted by other 
officers at different levels.  The Judicial Section of the Department of Legal Affairs defends 
Government of India in all Courts and Tribunals where Government of India is a party. The

litigation work of the Department in the Supreme Court of India is handled by the Central 
Agency Section (CAS), in High Cou rts and CAT (Principal Bench) by the Litigation (High 
Court), and in Subordinate Courts in Delhi by the Litigation (Lower Court) Section. 
1.5. The Department is also associated with appointment of law officers namely, Attorney 
General of India, Solicitor General of India and Additional Solicitor General of India. In 
addition, Government Counsels are also engaged to defend Government of India in various 
courts and tribunals across the country. It is responsible for maintenance of standards of legal 
profession and legal education and is associated with legal reforms also. It is also responsible 
for appointment and renewal of Notaries across the country. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, 
Indian Legal Service and Law Commission of India are within the administrative control of 
the Department. It is also responsible for signing and implementation of Treaties and 
Agreements with foreign countries in matters of civil law. 
1.6. The Department inter-alia administers the Advocates Act, 1961, the Advocates 
Welfare Fund Act, 2001, the Notaries Act 1952, the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, 
the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 and the New Delhi International Arbitration Centre Act, 
2019. It has also taken initiatives to improve India‟s ranking in 'Ease of Doing Business 
Report' (EODBR) of World Bank by strengthening contract enforcement and arbitration 
mechanism.  
1.7. Under the Digital India initiative, the Department has created a web based application 
namely, Legal Information Management & Briefing System (LIMBS) for monitoring of court 
cases at a single point and creation of a unified system to avoid confusion & delays and 
reduce financial burden on public exchequer. It has centralised database of more th an 5 lakh 
court cases in which Union of India is one of the party. 
1.8. Following Institutions/organizations are under the overall supervision of the 
Department of Legal Affairs:- 
(i) Law Commission of India (LCI): - The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory 
body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The term of Twenty-first Law 
Commission ended on 31st August, 2018. The Twenty-second Law Commission was 
constituted in February, 2020 for the term of three years from the date of publication of its 
order in the Gazette vide notification dated 21.02.2020. 
(ii) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): - ITAT is one of the oldest Tribunals, set up 
under Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to hear second appeals in all matters of direct 
taxes and appeals against the revision orders of Administrative Commissioners as well as 
orders denying registration under Section 12A or under Section 80G of the Income -tax Act 
1961. It functions as the final fact finding a uthority in the matters concerning Income -tax, 
wealth-tax, gift-tax etc. It has 63 Benches covering all cities having seats of High Courts.  
(iii) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body constituted 
under Section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and it has been empowered, among other things, 
to lay down standards for professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers, and to maintain and 
improve standards of legal education in the country.  

 
10 
(iv) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute is a premier legal research 
institute founded on 27th December, 1956. The prime objective of the Institute is to promote 
advanced studies and research in law and to contribute substantially in reforming the 
administration of justice, so as to meet the socio-economic aspirations of the people through 
law and its instrumentalities. The Institute has been granted Deemed University status in the 
year 2004. 
(v) The New Delhi International Arbitration Centre (NDIAC):- The New Delhi 
International Arbitration Centre (NDIAC), Act 2019 provides for the establishment and 
incorporation of the NDIAC as an independent and autonomous institution for arbitration and 
to make India a hub of institutional arbitration.

2.8. The Committee, further, notes that the salary is one of the major components of 
Secretariat expenditure of the Department for which it has been allocated Rs. 76.58 crore as

13 
2.9.  Further, as against the projection of Rs. 4.5 crore for BE (2022-23), Indian Law 
Institute (ILI) has been allocated Rs. 3.5 crore, which is an increase of Rs. 0.5 crore (16.66 
percent) over BE (2021-22) and a decrease of Rs. 6.5 crore (65 percent) over RE (2021-22).  
2.10. The Department has informed that funds  are  released  to  the  Indian  Law  Institute  
(ILI)  in  the  form of Grants-in-aid for utilisation against “Salary” and “General‟ purposes. 
The ILI being a grantee body, it is required to enhance its revenues to ensure long term self -
sustainability, and grants -in-aid are meant to support the activities of ILI to bridge the 
viability gaps. 
2.11. The Grants -in-aid (salary) to ILI partially cater to the funds requirement of ILI 
towards payment of salary and allowances, funds for Grants -in-aid (general) are provided to 
support its academic & research activit ies. In addition, from time to time the Department 
provides grants for special & specific purposes. The Department has informed that, the last 
such grant of Rs.1.00 crore was released in the financial year 2018 -19 towards the payment 
of arrears of 7 th Central Pay Commission recommendations. Similarly Rs. 6.50 crore has 
been provided to ILI in the current financial year (2021 -22) during the Revised Estimates 
(RE) as one time development grant for meeting outstanding and expedient funds 
requirement towards pa yment of property tax and physical building infrastructure. Thus, the 
reduced allocations in BE (2022 -23) due to one -time special grant in nature, in Financial 
Year (2021-22) shall not affect any major areas / projects of the ILI. 
2.12. The Department has informed that for the financial year 2021 -22 (up to 31.01.2022), 
it has already released grant -in-aid of Rs. 2.25 crore to ILI against the allocation of Rs 10.00 
crore. However, the Committee notes that till the last quarter of the financial year (2021 -22), 
the Department has released only 22.5 percent of the amount allocated to ILI. Further, in its 
written submission during the Demands for Grants (2022 -23), the ILI has informed that an 
expenditure of Rs.6.70 crore has already been incurred during current f inancial year towards 
payment of salaries and allowances to its employees. The ILI has submitted that it has been 
able to utilise 100 percent funds released to it by the Department of Legal Affairs during the 
last five years.  
2.13. The Department/ ILI has informed that over the last 5 years, 100 percent of funds 
released to ILI have been utilised and there was excess expenditure (50 percent 
approx.) of ILI vis-à-vis grants allocated for the same period. The ILI has informed this 
Committee that it has incurred an expenditure of Rs. 6.7 crore in the current financial 
year (as on 31.1.2022) towards payment of salaries and allowances. However, the 
Committee observes that  the ILI is not able to meet even its salary requirement for 
teaching and non -teaching staff from the grants allocated by the Department of Legal 
Affairs. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that ILI being a grantee institution 
should not eternally dep end on government grants and thus it needs to become self 
sufficient to meet its basic requirements. The Committee also feels that for the time 
being, grants-in-aid to ILI may be enhanced. The Committee, accordingly, recommends 
the Department to at least p rovide grants -in-aid to meet its 100 percent salary and 
allowances expenditure for sanctioned positions for the next five years. 
 

 
14 
2.14. The Committee observes that majority of earnings of ILI is from course fee 
charged from students/trainees, rent received  from Ministry of Law and Justice for 
leasing its premises, and interests. The Committee also observes that the pattern of 
earning has remained same for the last 2 -3 years, except some variations in financial 
year 2020 -21 due to Covid -19 pandemic. The Comm ittee is of the view that the ILI 
being a research Institution, needs to generate more and more funds from academic 
and consultancy activities, which are its core activities and not from rent/leasing its 
premises to Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the ILI to explore additional avenues to generate more funds 
from research/ consulting activities and gradually become self sufficient. 
2.15. The Committee also feels that ILI needs to expand its activities by way of 
introducing demand degrees/diploma programmes and consultancy activities by 
optimally utilising its existing infrastructure and accordingly, is of the view that its 
premises rented out to the Departments/institutions needs to be utilised for its own  
expansion. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to get the ILI 
premises vacated for its expansion. 
2.16. As per the Section 43 of the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019, the 
Arbitration Council of India (ACI) is proposed t o be an entity to promote institutional 
arbitration, frame  policies for grading arbitral institutions/accrediting arbitrators, 
maintenance of uniform professional standards for ADR matter and so forth so as to promote 
India as a hub of arbitration. However , the Department has not been able to appoint 
Chairperson and Members of the body till date which in turn has led non -utilisation of 
budgetary allocations meant for the purpose. 
2.17. The Committee observes that the Department was not able to spend a singl e 
Rupee from the allocations made under the head ACI in the Financial Year (2020-21) & 
(2021-22), however, it has again made a projection of Rs. 6.50 crore for the Financial 
Year (2022 -23) to the Ministry of Finance, against which Rs. 3.00 crore has been 
allocated in BE (2022 -23). In view of the above, the Committee feels that submission of 
Department that ACI allocations is primarily due to judicious expenditure in the 
Financial Year 2021 -22 and projection of optimum budget requirement in  Financial 
Year ( 2022-23), is not tenable. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the 
Department to expedite the appointment process of Chairperson, Members and 
Secretariat Staffs without further delay so that it become functional, and apprise the 
Committee about the timeline in this regard. 
2.18. Further, as against the projection of Rs. 9.00 crore for BE (2022-23), the New Delhi 
International Arbitration Centre (NDIAC) has been allocated Rs. 3.00 crore, which is an 
increase of Rs. 2.00 crore (200 percent) over BE and RE (2021-22). It can be observed that 
from the Financial Years 2020-21, including the current, the Department has not been able to 
spend a single Rupee, out of the fund allocated to NDIAC. 
 
2.19.  For the purpose of disbursement of salary to Chairperson/Members and other 
officers, the Centre had projected Rs. 3.00 crore in BE (2022 -23) against which Rs. 1.5 crore 
has been allocated. Further, for General purpose/administrative expenses and setting up 

 
15 
Arbitration Centre of internati onal standard, this Department had projected Rs. 6 crore (Rs.1 
crore for general purpose and Rs. 5 crore for setting up Arbitration Centre of international 
standard) against which an allocation of Rs. 1.5 crore has been made. The Department has 
submitted that additional funds may be required, and may be sought through supplementary 
demands for grants. 
 
2.20. The Department has informed that the process for establishment of New Delhi 
International Arbitration Centre (NDIAC) as a flagship institution for cond ucting 
international and domestic arbitration is in advance stage, and therefore, necessary provisions 
for salary and other administrative expenses for officers and staff of the NDIAC have been 
made in BE 2022-23. 
2.21.  The Committee is of the view that a rbitration processes are user friendly, cost 
effective, and expeditious as compared to litigation in courts. The New Delhi 
International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019 was enacted for the purpose of creating an 
independent and autonomous regime for instituti onalized arbitration in the country. 
The Committee in its previous reports, viz. 107th and 109 th had recommended for 
expediting the process of appointment of Chairperson and Members of NDIAC so as to 
promote institutional arbitration and make India a hub o f International Arbitration. 
However, more than 2.5 years have passed since the enactment of the NDIAC Act, rules 
for the same are yet to be finalised.  
2.22. The Committee observes that framing of rules are taking more time than the 
original Act itself, w hich may be due to bureaucratic quagmire.  The Committee 
expresses its concern for this inordinate delay in framing of rules and desires that the 
Department should apprise cogent reasons for not following the recommendations of 
the Committee. 
2.23. The Com mittee also observes that the Department has also not been able to 
spend a single rupee out of the funds allocated from the Financial Years 2020 -21 
onwards; it has sought exponentially higher allocations. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends that the Dep artment in future needs to rationally project its demand 
under the head NDIAC.

CHAPTER - III 
 POLICY ISSUES PERTAINING TO THE DEPARTMENT 
3.0 The Department of Legal Affairs is a service-oriented Department and the Budget of 
the Department is mainly salary-based. It has been entrusted with the work of providing 
advice to Ministries on legal matters including interpretation of the Constitution and the laws, 
engagement of counsels to appear on behalf of the Union of India in Supreme Court, High 
Courts and Subordinate Courts where the Union of India is a party.

Courts, Tribunals and District and Subordinate Courts.  The Department is also concerned 
with appointment of Notaries and renewal of Notary certificates. The budgetary allocations 
include expenditure for Branch Secretariats of the Department, Central Agency Section, 
Income-Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), New Delhi International Arbitration Centre, Law 
Commission of India (LCI), payment to Legal Advisers and Counsels and Grants-in-aid to 
the Indian Law Institute (ILI).  The budgetary allocations to the Department have already 
been discussed in Chapter-II of this report.

Empanelment of Counsels 
3.17. There are three categories of Law Officers appointed by the Department, i.e., 
Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India, and Additional Solicitors General of 
India (ASGI). In addition, the Department also empanels Counsels for Central Government 
litigation in High Courts and tribunals. 
3.18. The Department has further informed that there is no criteria/ methodology to project 
the required number of panel counsels for a court/tribunal. However, keeping in view the size 
of High Court, number of Central Government litigations and so forth, appropriate number of 
counsel are engaged with  the approval of Hon‟ble Minister for Law & Justice on the basis of 
their interest, qualification, experience, reputation, expertise, professional competence and 
standing at Bar, and interviews are not conducted for this purpose. Further, 
empanelment/engagement of Advocates as panel counsel is an ongoing process and 
projecting actual total number of panel counsel for a High Court on an earlier date is not 
feasible due to expiry of terms, deaths and resignation etc. The High Court -wise details of 
panel counsel empanelled by this Department is at Annexure-I.  As on 10 th January, 2022, 
the Department has spent Rs. 32.54 crore towards payment of fee to Government 
advocates/Panel counsels in various High Courts and tribunals in the Financial Year 2021-22. 
3.19. The Committee observes that the Department has not devised any 
criteria/methodology to project the required number of panel counsels for a Court/ 
Tribunal. Further, th ere is no information available on the Department’s website with 
regard to empanelment process of panel counsels. The Committee, accordingly, feels 
that the Department needs to devise a rational methodology for projecting required 
number of panel counsels/ advocates based on the number of institution/pending cases, 
nature of cases and so forth to ensure transparency and optimal utilisation of 
government resources. The details of empanelment process/criteria also need to be 
uploaded in the Department’s websit e for the benefit of potential candidates applying 
for empanelment as government/panel counsels.

3.20. There are large numbers of cases pending in various courts and tribunals in the 
country. On the questionnaire of the Committ ee on pendency of government cases in various 
High Courts, the Department submitted that it doesn‟t have details of total number of court 
cases where government is a party, however, it informed that details of Central Government 
cases are updated on LEGAL Information Management & Briefing System (LIMBS) portal 
by the 57 user Ministries/Departments. Data on LIMBS portal is user based which is entered 
by user of respective Ministry/Department and not centrally by the Department of Legal 
Affairs. As per the da ta provided by the Department, there are around 5.88 lakh government 
cases pending in various courts/tribunals. The Department has also informed that as per the 
information available with it, there are 2,222 contempt of court cases pending against various 
Ministries/ Departments (Annexure-II). 
3.21. The Department has informed that several measures have been undertaken by the 
concerned Department/Ministry to reduce pendency of cases. Ministry of Railways has laid 
emphasis on strict monitoring of court cases . Further, Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) 

 
22 
and Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) have enhanced monetary threshold 
for filing appeals. 
3.22.  The Committee appreciates the Department for creating LIMBS portal for 
monitoring of government litigations in courts and tribunals and also initiatives of some 
Ministries/Department like Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Railways to reduce 
litigations. However, the Committee also observes that still large numbers of 
government cases are pending  in various courts and tribunals, and accordingly, feels 
that monetary threshold for filing appeals may be gradually enhanced to avoid 
unnecessary appeals.  
3.23. With regard to large number of contempt cases against various Ministries, the 
Committee fails  to understand as to why there are so many contempt cases against 
government Departments/Ministries. The Committee feels that the Department need to 
prepare broad guidelines/policy for filing cases/appeals so as to limit discretions of 
government officials  dealing with cases for filing appeal after appeal leading to 
contempt cases, thereby wasting government resources. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Department to frame guidelines/policy for filing cases/appeals in court 
cases and also sensitize the Departments/Ministries in this regard to reduce contempt 
cases.

Indian Law Institute (ILI) 
3.31. The Indian Law Institute is a deemed university promoting advanced studies and 
research in law and also contributing in reforming the administration of justice. It is the only 
Institution imparting legal research along with higher education in legal field established 
under administrative control of Ministry of Law and Justice. Research is one of the major 
focal point of ILI, and it has encouraged its faculties to take up research activities in 
interdisciplinary and contemporary issues. ILI has a lso provided consultancy services to the 
Ministry of Law & Justice on various occasions.  
3.32. At present, it has the sanctioned strength of 95 posts (20 teaching and 75 non -
teaching), however, the existing strength is only 43 (7 teaching posts and 36 non -teaching 
posts).  The teaching posts include Director (01), Senior Professor (01), Professor (02) and 
Assistant Professor (03). 
 
3.33. The ILI has submitted that existing strength of teaching and non -teaching posts are 
sufficient to meet the present requirement as the Institute is presently running only one batch 
of LL.M. (One Year) Programme consisting of 40 students along with four Even ing Diploma 
Courses and Ph.D. Programme. Numbers of Courses in ILI were reduced to focus on research 
activities, which is the main objective of the Institute. The institute has advertised for filling -
up various posts in December, 2019, however, due to Covi d-19 the recruitment process 
couldn‟t be completed.

3.34. The Committee observes that out of the sanctioned 20 teaching posts, only 7 
posts (35 percent) are filled -up. Further, out of 75 non teaching posts, only 36 are in 
position (48 Percent). The Committee is not convinced with the argument of the ILI that 
existing strength of teaching and non -teaching posts is sufficient to meet the present 
requirement and is of the unanimous view that for the ILI to function at its optimal 
level, it will have to fill -up the vacant positions of teaching and non -teaching staffs. The 
Committee also feels that ILI may explore the feasibility of introducing post -doctoral 
research fellowships to young legal researchers on emerging legal areas. 
3.35. During the meeting of the C ommittee on the Demands for Grants (2022 -23), the 
Director of ILI requested this Committee to recommend the government for granting Institute 
of National Importance (INI) to ILI, as except in legal field, almost all other fields already 
have institutions with INI status. The Director, ILI also submitted that the existing grants -in –
aid is not sufficient to meet the salary and recurring expenses of the institution and requested 
for enhancement of grants. The Department of Legal Affairs, in its written submis sion has 
informed this Committee that the criteria for awarding the status of INI and the particular 
benefits institutions receive on getting this status are not mentioned in any document. 
3.36. The Committee in its previous Reports has observed that ILI n eeds to expand its 
activities and also needs to expand itself to other parts of the country also by establishing 
extension centers in cities like Chennai, Mumbai, Guwahati, and so forth. The Committee in 
its 96 th, 101 st and 105 th Reports had discussed the issue of granting of Institute of National 
Importance status to ILI. 
3.37. There are Institutions of National Importance in India in every field of education and 
research, viz., Architecture, Design, Engineering and Technology, Food Technology, 
Management, Medicine and Pharmacy, except Legal education and research. Those are, like 
IITs, IIMs, NITs, IIITs, SPAs, IISERs  (under MoE), NIPERs (under Ministry of Chemicals 
and Fertilisers), NIDs (under Ministry of Commerce and Industry), RGIPT (under Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas), NIFTEMs (under Ministry of Food Processing Industries) and 
AIIMSs (under Ministry of Health and Family Welfare).   
3.38. The Committee observes that Institution of National Importance (INI) status has 
been granted to institution s imparting education in engineering, design, medicine, 
science, pharmacy  and so forth, however, no such status has been granted to institution 
imparting dedicated law/legal education. The Committee feels that the ILI deserves to 
flourish under the umbrella of an Institution of National Importance in the field of legal 
education and research, through appropriate enactment by the Parliament. This will 
help in furthering legal education and research dimensions at a global platform through 
the legacy earned by the Indian Law Institute. The Committee is of the view that a time 
bound action must be taken in this regard. In the light of the above, the Committee 
recommends that the Department of Legal Affairs should take appropriate steps to 
bring a draft enactmen t in Parliament for empowering the Indian Law Institute as an 
Institution of National Importance (INI) in line with other INIs of various other 
Ministries.

3.39. The Law Commission of India is a statutory body constituted from time  to time for 
the purpose to review / repeal of obsolete laws and makes its recommendations to 
Government for repeal of obsolete laws and for appropriate amendments in others as may be 
found necessary.  
3.40. The Department of Legal Affairs during the meeting on Demands for Grants (2022 -
23) had informed that the Commission will commence its functioning once appointment of 
the Chairman and Members of the Commission are made, which is under process. Further, in

the appointment of Chairman a nd Member(s) of 22nd Law Commission of India is under 
consideration of the Government. 
3.41. The Union Cabinet approved the constitution of the 22nd Law Commission of 
India and Gazette notification for the same was published on the 21st February, 2020. 
However, the Committee observes that even after more than two years of its 
constitution, the appointment processes of Chairperson and Members of the 
Commission is yet to be completed. The Committee is disappointed with the snail’s pace 
of their appointment processes, as a body whose tenure itself is three years is now in its 
3rd year without a Chairperson and Members. The Committee fails to understand that 
why post of Chairperson and Members are vacant for such a longtime in such an 
important body like Law Commission. 
3.42. The Committee feels that since more than two and half ye ars have already 
elapsed, appointment of Chairman and Members for the remainder would not serve the 
desired purpose. The Committee desires that the Chairman and Members of the LCI 
may be appointed for full -term of three years, instead of the remaining peri od from the

Bar Council of India (BCI) 
3.46. The Bar Council of India (BCI) is a statutory body constituted under the Advocates 
Act, 1961, which has been empowered among other things to lay down standards of 
professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers, maintain and improve the standard of legal 
education in the country and enforce discipline among the lawyers. The BCI also acts as an 
appellate authority in respect of disciplinary matters.  
3.47.  As on date more than 4.77 crore cases are pending in various courts and there 23 lakh 
lawyers in the country. The Bar Council of India (BCI) in its written submission before the 
Committee on the Demands for Grants (2022-23) has informed the Committee that lawyers 
in the country neither have any social security nor any protection from either State of Union 
Government. There is also lack of proper infrastructure and other facilities like sitting space, 
clean drinking water, electricity, libraries, medical aid, health insurance etc. for advocates in 
various courts.  
3.48. The BCI has further submitted that due to lack of funds, Bar Associations are not in a 
position to purchase law journals, computers, wifi facilities and so forth, which hinders 
practice of law. The BCI has also highlighted the plight of advocates due to Covid-19 and 
has submitted that many advocates have died and dependents of advocates are facing acute 
financial problems affecting their livelihood. The BCI requested this Committee to consider 
recommending grants for the purpose through Bar Councils/Associations in order to carry 
out the welfare activities and also to meet the medical aid, health insurance facilities, and 
also library/other infrastructure facilities of Bar Associations. 
3.49. On the allocations of grants-in-aid/funds to the BCI, the Department of Legal Affairs 
has submitted that no grants have been released to BCI in the last 10 years as BCI has 
apparently not made any request for grants having achieved the self-sustainability financially. 
The last grants-in-aid were released amounting to Rs.6.0 lakh and Rs. 1.88 lakh to BCI in the 
financial year 2010-11 and 2009-10 respectively. While the grant in 2010-11 was given for 
restructuring of professional & legal education standards, the grants-in-aid in 2009-10 was 
released for the purpose of donation of books to Junior Advocates/ deserving Bar 
Associations.  

 
28 
3.50. The BCI has also informed that around Rs. 1 lakh expenditure is involved in 
disposing a single disciplinary matter involving advocates, whereas the fees given by parties 
is only Rs. 2000. The BCI generates funds from inspection of colleges, advocates enrolment 
fee and so forth. To verify fake degrees/certificates the Bar Council of India framed “Bar 
Council of India Certificate and Place of Practice (Verification) Rules, 2015”. Further, the 
Supreme Court of India (2017) also directed universities to verify degrees of advocates 
enrolled in various State Bar Councils without charging any fee. However, the BCI informed 
that 90 percent Universities are not verifying or responding to the queries made by the 
various State Bar Councils and due to non co-operation of the Universities the Bar Council of 
India is feeling difficulty in weeding out the fake degree holders. 
3.51. As regards release of grants-in-aid/funds to BCI for the financial year 2022-23, the 
Department submitted that any Institution/Organisation seeking Grants-in-aid from 
Government is required to submit an application which includes all relevant information such 
as Articles of Association, bye-laws, audited statement of accounts, sources and pattern of 
income and expenditure etc. enabling the sanctioning authority to assess the suitability of the 
Institution/Organisation seeking Grant. Further, the Department has informed that no such 
application seeking Grants-in-aid has been received from the BCI; and there is no proposal 
for release of grants to BCI. 
3.52. The Committee observes from the submissions made by both the Department of 
Legal Affairs and Bar Council of India that the Department releases grants only after 
receiving request from concerned organisation/Institution and no such application for 
seeking grants has been received from the BCI, hence there is no proposal for release of 
Grants to BCI by the Department. The Committee was apprised of the plight of lawyers 
due to covid -19 pandemic by BCI and infrastructural constraints of Bar 
Councils/Associations and request for recommending grants, including provisions for  
medical aid, health insurance etc. to undertake welfare activities. 
3.53. The Committee observes from the submission of the BCI that many Bar 
Associations, especially in rural areas require proper infrastructure and basic amenities 
like toilets, drinking water, fans, good library for facilitating good practice of Advocacy, 
computers with internet facilitie s and proper sitting space for Advocates and their 
clients, and is of the view that  without a conducive atmosphere, the justice system 
suffers and leads to delays and pendency of cases.  The Committee feels that BCI needs 
to be provided with some grants by  the Department for basic infrastructural and other 
facilities like sitting space, clean drinking water, electricity, libraries, etc. in various 
courts, and accordingly, recommends the Bar Council of India to approach the 
Department of Legal Affairs for Gr ants-in –aid. The Committee also feels that the 
Department may approach the Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice for 
exploring the feasibility of recommending grants/or including infrastructure facilities 
for Bar Associations  under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of 
Infrastructure Facilities for Districts and Subordinate Judiciary . The Committee, 
further, recommends the Department of Legal Affairs to explore the feasibility of 
providing grants to the BCI and also submit a  status note to this Committee while 
furnishing Action Taken Replies on the issue along with appropriate justifications.  

 
29 
3.54. The Committee also feels that budgetary allocations for Welfare of Advocates 
during pandemic and natural calamities may be made in the budget allocation, and 
there should also be provisions to disburse interest free /low interest loans. It also feels 
that that there is a requirement for life/term insurance and health insurance as well as 
for nominal/subsidized medical facilities fo r majority of Advocates and their families, 
who are under financial duress, more so, due to the pandemic. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Department to explore available options and modalities in 
this regard and submit a status note while submitting the action taken replies. 
3.55. As per Section 49(d) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the BCI is empowered to makes 
rules to regulate standards of legal education to be observed by Universities in India and the 
inspection of Universities for that purpose. The BCI Rules of Legal Education lays  down 
standards of professional legal education in the country. The Committee was informed that 
Bar Council of India has taken initiative to further raise the standards of Legal Education and 
Legal Profession by seeking to establish a Teachers Training Aca demy and Advocate 
Professional Skill Development Programme and further University of Legal Education of 
International repute.   
3.56. The Committee notes that there is mushrooming of law colleges/institutions across 
the country with poor infrastructure facilities and law teachers in the last few years. The BCI 
has informed that they have a team to inspect law universities/colleges. The BCI in its 
written replies to the questionnaire of the Committee has informed that in the last three years 
it inspected 296 (2019), 39(2020), and 158(2021) universities/colleges in the country. It 
further informed that between the years 2017 to 2021, it derecognized/submitted adverse 
remarks against 119 universities/colleges. 
 
3.57. With regard to malpractices in granting r ecognition to law colleges, the BCI 
submitted that, the Legal Education Committee of Bar Council of India has constituted 
surprise Visiting Teams headed by former High Court Judges, which includes only the Law 
Teachers/Professors.  These Visiting Teams vis its sub-standard law colleges of the country, 
earmarked by the Bar Council of India and as per the planning, all such sub -standard colleges 
who are involved in distribution of fake degrees in connivance with various Universities are 
to be closed down in coming six months.  It is to be noted that ensuring/marking attendance is 
the duty of the Institution/University.  Similarly, the fair examination is the duty of the 
University and the Bar Council of India or any State Bar Council has no control over these 
affairs of the Universities.  Therefore, the Bar Council of India cannot be blamed for 
degradation of the standard of Legal Education of the Country. 
3.58. With regard to All India Bar Examination (AIBE), the BCI informed that it is being 
conducted for candidates who have obtained their law degree from the academic years 2009-
10 onwards. As per the original AIBE Rules, advocates enrolled in the State Bar Council 
were only to practice in the court of law after passing this examination. However, over the 
years the BCI relaxed those rules and provisionally allowed advocates to practice for two 
years from the date of enrolment with a condition that they should pass the exam within two 
years. The BCI in August, 2020 further extended and relaxed its rules and allowed advocates 
to continue in practice without passing the AIBE for few more years. 

 
30 
 
3.59. The Committee appreciates the Bar Council of India’s initiative to improve the 
standards of legal education, however, it is of the view that utmost care must be taken 
in granting recognition to law colleges/institutions to impart legal education across the 
country. The Committee observes that legal education is being commercialized and 
many colleges without having proper class room, building, library etc. and ghost 
teachers are granting law degrees and candidates without attending law classes are 
enrolling as advocates thereby increasing the pool of sub-standard lawyers. 
 
3.60. The Committee also feels that the BCI also needs to improve the standard of All 
India Bar Examinations (AIBE) and accordingly recommends that exit examination to 
practice law in the country should be made compulsory without any further 
relaxations. Further, the Committee is of the strong view that to enhance the quality of 
legal education and preserve the credibility of legal profession, the BCI needs to 
improve its regulatory functions and therefore, law universities promoting malpractices 
needs to be strictly dealt with.  
 
3.61. The Committee also feels that as part of improving the legal education and 
profession in the country, the BCI may explore the options of revisiting the earlier 
practice of compulsory apprenticeship of law graduates, and Department/BCI should 
apprise the Committee about their considered opinion on the issue.
